sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.summary: Introduces Chapter 6 on seepage and drainage, covering methods for analyzing seepage in soils and bedrock, design guidance for drainage elements, internal erosion mechanisms, and mitigation strategies. Establishes scope as saturated seepage only and outlines three fundamental mitigation strategies: blocking/lengthening pathways, controlled drainage, and filtering.
key_points: Chapter covers seepage analysis methods, internal erosion mechanisms, and seepage/drainage mitigation for structures and foundations.
Seepage is driven by differential hydraulic head and flows from higher to lower potential energy.
Scope is limited to saturated flow conditions; unsaturated flow above the water table is excluded.
Undesirable seepage consequences include internal erosion, excessive water loss or accumulation, and excess pore water pressures.
Three basic mitigation strategies: (1) block/lengthen seepage pathway, (2) drain excess water pressures in a controlled manner, (3) filter seepage to prevent particle transport.
sections.applicability: Applies whenever seepage analysis or drainage design is required for soils, bedrock, structures, or foundations under saturated conditions.

sections.title: Scope
sections.summary: Defines the scope of Chapter 6 as covering methods for analyzing seepage in soils and bedrock, design guidance for drainage elements, summaries of seepage analysis methods, descriptions of internal erosion mechanisms, and discussion of seepage and internal erosion mitigation methods.
sections.body: This chapter discusses methods for analyzing seepage in soils and bedrock and provides design guidance for drainage elements in structures and foundations. The chapter provides a summary of available methods for analyzing the seepage regime, descriptions and analysis methods for internal erosion mechanisms, and discussion of seepage and internal erosion mitigation methods.
key_points: Chapter addresses both seepage analysis methods and drainage element design.
Internal erosion mechanisms are described and analysis methods are provided.
Mitigation methods for seepage and internal erosion are discussed.
sections.applicability: Applies as a scope statement for all geotechnical seepage and drainage design covered in Chapter 6.

sections.title: Background
sections.summary: Provides background on seepage as flow through interstitial voids of soil or rock driven by differential hydraulic head. Discusses common geotechnical seepage contexts, limits scope to saturated conditions, identifies undesirable consequences (internal erosion, excessive water loss, excess pore pressures), and outlines three mitigation strategies.
sections.body: Seepage is the flow of water through interstitial voids of soil or rock. Seepage is driven by differential potential energy of water (i.e., hydraulic head) acting across the soil or rock mass, resulting in the flow of water from higher to lower potential energy. Seepage is a common phenomenon in geotechnical engineering applications and can occur as natural groundwater flow, seepage through dams and levees or their foundations, or flow into excavations extending below the groundwater surface. While the movement of water occurs in unsaturated soils above the groundwater table, this chapter deals only with seepage that occurs under saturated conditions. Undesirable consequences of seepage can include internal erosion, excessive water loss or accumulation, and excessive pore water pressures. Under the right conditions, seepage can result in erosion of soil or rock, or internal erosion. Several different mechanisms of internal erosion have been identified that can occur by one of several mechanisms. In cases where seepage quantities are large, problems can occur, including: excessive water loss from reservoirs, flooding of excavations, and unstable ground due to excess moisture. Seepage may also result in excess water pressures under structures leading to instability and uplift forces. This chapter also discusses a number of strategies and methods for mitigating the undesirable effects of seepage discussed in the previous paragraph. Each method utilizes one or a combination of three basic strategies: 1) blocking or lengthening the seepage pathway, 2) draining the excess water pressures in a controlled manner, and 3) filtering the seepage to block the transportation of soil particles.
key_points: Seepage is flow through interstitial voids driven by differential hydraulic head (potential energy).
Common seepage contexts include natural groundwater flow, dams, levees, and excavations below the water table.
Chapter scope is limited to saturated seepage; unsaturated flow is excluded.
Undesirable consequences: internal erosion, excessive water loss from reservoirs, excavation flooding, excess pore pressures, uplift forces.
Three mitigation strategies: block/lengthen seepage path, controlled drainage of excess pressures, filter seepage to prevent particle transport.
sections.applicability: Applies as background context for all seepage-related analyses and design decisions in Chapter 6.

sections.title: SEEPAGE ANALYSES
sections.summary: Parent section for all seepage analysis methods in Chapter 6, encompassing hydraulic head fundamentals, Darcy's Law, two-dimensional seepage theory, flow nets, closed-form equations, and numerical seepage analysis. Covers the full range of tools from graphical to advanced numerical methods for characterizing flow regimes.
key_points: Covers the full spectrum of seepage analysis tools: hydraulic head concepts, Darcy's Law, flow nets, closed-form methods, and numerical FEA.
Methods range from hand-drawn graphical solutions to finite element analysis for complex geometries.
Graphical and analytical methods serve as important validation tools for numerical models.
sections.applicability: Applies whenever a seepage regime must be analyzed for any geotechnical structure or foundation condition.

sections.title: Hydraulic Head
sections.summary: Defines total hydraulic head as the sum of pressure head and elevation head (velocity head negligible in geologic media), expressed in length units relative to a datum. Explains the physical meaning using piezometers and a pressurized tank example, and establishes Eq. 6-1 as the governing expression for total head used throughout all seepage analyses.
sections.body:
Hydraulic head is a measure of the energy of the water acting on or within geologic media, expressed in terms of length units and referenced to a consistent datum. The total hydraulic head (ht) at any given point is composed of three components: the pressure head (hp), the elevation head (hz), and the velocity head (hv). In geologic media, the velocity head is typically negligible and the total head is expressed as:

ht = hp + hz = u/γw + z  (6-1)

where: u = the water pressure at the point of interest, γw = the unit weight of water, and z = the elevation of the point of interest above the elevation datum.

The total hydraulic head (ht) at a point is the height above the elevation datum that water would rise in a piezometer if the tip of that piezometer were located at the point of interest as illustrated in Figure 6-1a. The total hydraulic head will vary within a flow regime unless conditions are completely static (i.e., no flow is occurring).

As an example, consider the pressurized tank in Figure 6-1b. Piezometers have been set at two points in the side of the tank and the water rises in the piezometer above the elevation of the tank due to the pressure in the tank. The pressure head (hp) is the height that the water rises above the point of interest and the elevation head (hz) is the height of the point of interest above the datum that has been set below the tank. The total head (ht) is the combined heights of hp and hz and is the total height that the water rises above the set datum. Since there is no flow within the tank, ht is constant throughout the tank although hp and hz vary with elevation.
key_points: Total hydraulic head = pressure head + elevation head; velocity head is negligible in geologic media.
Eq. 6-1: ht = u/γw + z, where u is water pressure, γw is unit weight of water, z is elevation above datum.
Total head physically equals the height water rises in a piezometer above the elevation datum.
In static conditions (no flow), total head is constant throughout the system even though pressure and elevation heads vary.
A consistent elevation datum must be established and referenced throughout seepage analysis.

equations.description: Total hydraulic head as sum of pressure head and elevation head: ht = hp + hz = u/γw + z

sections.applicability: Applies whenever hydraulic head must be defined or calculated at any point within a seepage flow regime in soil or rock.

sections.title: Darcy's Law and One-Dimensional Flow
sections.summary: Presents Darcy's Law for one-dimensional seepage flow, defining hydraulic gradient, volumetric flow rate, discharge velocity, and seepage velocity. Establishes Equations 6-2 through 6-6 as the governing relationships. Notes that Darcy's Law is valid for laminar flow, which covers most soil seepage, but may overestimate flow in coarse open-graded gravels where turbulent conditions arise.
sections.body:
The principles of seepage mechanics and analysis of the seepage regime are best illustrated by considering the example of one-dimensional flow illustrated schematically in Figure 6-2. A soil-filled conduit with a cross section of area (A) and a length (L) is attached to water reservoirs with different total heads. The difference in water height in piezometers at each end of the conduit indicates the differential total head (hL) or head loss across the soil. This head also represents the amount of energy that must be dissipated as the water flows through the soil. The differential head creates a hydraulic gradient (i), which is defined as:

i = hL / L  (6-2)

where: i = the hydraulic gradient, hL = the differential total head (or head loss), and L = the length over which hL occurs.

The hydraulic gradient forces the water to flow through the soil at a volumetric flow rate (q) that is sufficient to create the head loss associated with hL. The volumetric flow rate is defined as the flow volume that passes through the soil per unit of time.

One-dimensional flow is governed by Darcy's Law:

q = kiA  (6-3)

where: q = the volumetric flow rate through the soil, k = the hydraulic conductivity of the soil, i = the hydraulic gradient across the flow region, and A = the cross sectional area of the flow region perpendicular to the flow direction.

If the flow region has a constant height and an extended width (perpendicular to the page), the flow area (A) can be defined by the height of the flow region times a unit width. In this case, the flow rate per unit length of the model is:

q = kiy  (6-4)

where: q = the flow rate per unit length of the model, k = the hydraulic conductivity of the soil, i = the hydraulic gradient across the flow region, and y = the height of the flow region.

The discharge velocity (vd) can be calculated by dividing the volumetric flow rate by the cross-sectional area:

vd = q/A = ki  (6-5)

It should be noted that vd is not a true particle velocity but rather the velocity based on the total area of the flow region. Since the water only flows through the pore space of a soil or rock, a water particle actually flows faster through than vd. The seepage velocity (vs) which measures how fast a water particle moves as a result of the hydraulic gradient, is calculated as:

vs = vd/n = vd(1+e)/e  (6-6)

where: n = the porosity of the soil and e = void ratio.

Darcy's law is valid for conditions where the seepage flow is laminar, which includes most cases of seepage through soils. High velocity flows through coarse, open-graded gravels may fall in the transition between laminar and turbulent flow. Turbulent flow results in more resistance to seepage and thus a lower volumetric flow rate than predicted by Darcy's law.
key_points: Hydraulic gradient i = hL/L (Eq. 6-2); represents energy dissipated per unit length of flow path.
Darcy's Law: q = kiA (Eq. 6-3); volumetric flow rate is proportional to hydraulic conductivity, gradient, and area.
For unit-width 2D models: q = kiy (Eq. 6-4), where y is the height of the flow region.
Discharge velocity vd = ki (Eq. 6-5) is NOT the true particle velocity; it is based on total cross-sectional area.
Seepage velocity vs = vd/n (Eq. 6-6) represents actual water particle movement through pore space; always greater than vd.
Darcy's Law assumes laminar flow; may overestimate flow in coarse, open-graded gravels where turbulent flow can occur.

equations.description: Hydraulic gradient: i = hL / L, where hL is head loss and L is the length over which it occurs.
Darcy's Law for volumetric flow rate: q = kiA, where k is hydraulic conductivity, i is hydraulic gradient, A is cross-sectional area.
Flow rate per unit length of model: q = kiy, where y is the height of the flow region.
Discharge velocity: vd = q/A = ki; velocity based on total cross-sectional area, not true particle velocity.
Seepage velocity: vs = vd/n = vd(1+e)/e; actual velocity of water particles through pore space.

sections.applicability: Applies to one-dimensional seepage flow problems in soils under laminar flow conditions, including flow through conduits, layers, and simple foundation configurations.

sections.title: Two-Dimensional Seepage
sections.summary: Introduces the LaPlace equation (Eq. 6-7) as the governing equation for steady-state two-dimensional seepage, derived from conservation of mass applied to a soil element. Identifies three solution approaches: graphical (flow nets), closed-form (method of fragments, blanket theory), and numerical (finite element). References Bear (1979) and Freeze and Cherry (1979) for derivation details.
sections.body:
Analysis of seepage in a two-dimensional regime requires expansion of Darcy's law. The governing equation for steady state, two-dimensional flow is the LaPlace equation:

∂²h/∂x² + ∂²h/∂y² = 0  (6-7)

where: h = total hydraulic head and x and y = coordinate directions.

The LaPlace equation is derived by applying the conservation of mass principle to an element of soil, thereby using equilibrium to spatially link changes in total head within the flow region. The first term in Equation (6-7) represents the change in hydraulic gradient in the x direction through an element of soil while the second term represents the change in gradient in the y direction in the same element. Derivation and further discussion of the LaPlace equation can be found in books on groundwater, such as Bear (1979) or Freeze and Cherry (1979).

Solutions to the LaPlace equation can be performed through (1) graphical solutions such as flow nets, (2) closed-form equations such as the method of fragments or the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers blanket theory equations (USACE 2000), or (3) numerical solutions such as finite element analyses.
key_points: Governing equation for steady-state 2D seepage is the LaPlace equation: ∂²h/∂x² + ∂²h/∂y² = 0 (Eq. 6-7).
Derived from conservation of mass applied to a soil element; spatially links total head changes.
Three solution approaches: (1) graphical flow nets, (2) closed-form (method of fragments, blanket theory), (3) numerical FEA.
LaPlace equation assumes isotropic, homogeneous permeability; modifications required for anisotropic soils.

equations.description: LaPlace equation for steady-state two-dimensional seepage: ∂²h/∂x² + ∂²h/∂y² = 0.

sections.applicability: Applies whenever seepage must be analyzed in a two-dimensional flow regime under steady-state saturated conditions.

sections.title: Flow Nets
sections.summary: Describes flow nets as a graphical solution tool for two-dimensional seepage analysis requiring only pencil, paper, and eraser. Introduces the concept of flow channels, equipotential lines, and flow lines using an example beneath an impermeable dam. Explains that drawing flow nets builds deeper engineering understanding than numerical analysis alone.
sections.body:
Flow nets are a relatively quick graphical solution tool for analyzing two-dimensional flow regimes using few resources; namely a pencil, paper, and a good eraser. The act of drawing of a flow net also helps the engineer to visualize and understand the behavior of seepage flows. The understanding gained by drawing a flow net is often deeper than that gained by numerical analyses.

A flow net for seepage in an isotropic soil layer beneath an impermeable dam is presented in Figure 6-3. The flow region is divided into flow elements, most of which resemble squares or are as close to square as possible. The long-short dashed lines represent equipotential lines or contours of constant total head within the soil. Note that the level upstream ground surface is an equipotential line since the reservoir level applies a constant total head along this boundary. The level downstream ground surface is also an equipotential line since the pressure is constant on the surface (equal to zero pressure head) and the elevation is constant (constant elevation head). If the downstream exit face were sloped and not submerged, the total head would not be constant and it would not be an equipotential line. The short dashed lines are flow lines, which represent average paths that water particles will follow while flowing through the soil. The bottom impervious boundary and the bottom of the impervious structure are also flow lines.
key_points: Flow nets are a graphical solution to the LaPlace equation requiring minimal resources and building deep engineering intuition.
Flow elements in a valid flow net resemble curvilinear squares; a circle can be inscribed touching all four boundaries.
Equipotential lines are contours of constant total head; flow lines represent average particle flow paths.
Level submerged boundaries are equipotential lines; impervious boundaries act as flow lines.
Drawing flow nets helps engineers understand seepage behavior more deeply than numerical analysis alone.
sections.applicability: Applies when a quick, resource-efficient graphical seepage analysis is needed for two-dimensional flow in isotropic or transformable anisotropic soils.

sections.title: Drawing Flow Nets
sections.summary: Provides the construction rules and resulting characteristics for valid flow nets, including orthogonality of flow and equipotential lines, curvilinear square flow elements, boundary conditions for impermeable surfaces and submerged boundaries, treatment of phreatic surfaces, and handling of non-homogeneous and anisotropic soil profiles including the anisotropic transformation factor (Eq. 6-8).
sections.body:
Flow nets for seepage through soil with isotropic permeability must comply with the following rules in order to be correct:
a. Flow lines and equipotential lines should intersect at right angles.
b. The flow elements formed between the flow lines and equipotential should resemble curvilinear squares. A circle can be inscribed in a curvilinear square and touch all four boundaries of the flow element. More guidance on the shape of admissible flow elements can be found in USACE (1986).
c. An impermeable boundary will act as a flow line. Common examples are the top of an underlying layer and the bottom of an impermeable dam or levee.
d. Submerged inflow or outflow boundaries through which seepage passes are equipotential lines with head equal to the water level elevation.
e. Where the flow is unconfined (such as through an embankment) the top flow line will be the phreatic surface. Points on this line will have pressure equal to zero and, consequently, the total head is equal to the elevation of the line (see Equation 6-1).
f. Along a phreatic surface for unconfined flow, equipotential lines will intercept the phreatic surface at equal vertical intervals.

Flow nets constructed according to the above rules will have the following characteristics:
a. Each flow channel, bounded by two adjacent flow lines, will convey the same amount of flow as the other flow channels in the flow net.
b. Each total head drop, bounded by two adjacent equipotential lines, represents the same decrease in total head as the other head drops in the flow net.
c. The flow elements can be subdivided into regions representing partial head drops and partial flow channels.

Flow nets can be drawn for flow through non-homogenous soil profiles and soil with anisotropic hydraulic conductivity. In stratified soil profiles, the flow will be dominated by the permeable layers. If the ratio of a layer's hydraulic conductivity compared to that of the most permeable layer exceeds 10 to 100, the layer can be considered impermeable. If this ratio is less than 10, the flow will be through both layers. However, the flow lines and equipotential lines will be deflected at the interface as illustrated in Figure 6-4.

Flow through soil with anisotropic permeability can be transformed into an equivalent isotropic region using the transformation factor (a):

a = √(kmax/kmin)  (6-8)

where: a = isotropic transformation factor, kmax = the maximum hydraulic conductivity in anisotropic soil, and kmin = the minimum hydraulic conductivity in anisotropic soil.

The dimensions of the flow region are transformed by dividing all of the dimensions of parallel to the direction of kmax by a. A flow net is drawn for the transformed system following the rules for isotropic hydraulic conductivity. For example, if k is largest in the horizontal direction, then all of the x-coordinates will be divided by a in the transformed system. If needed, the flow region and flow net can be transformed back to 'real space' by multiplying the dimensions parallel to the direction of kmax by a.
key_points: Flow lines and equipotential lines must intersect at right angles; flow elements must be curvilinear squares.
Impermeable boundaries act as flow lines; submerged inflow/outflow boundaries are equipotential lines.
For unconfined flow, the phreatic surface is the top flow line with zero pressure; equipotential lines intercept it at equal vertical intervals.
Each flow channel carries equal flow; each head drop between equipotential lines is equal.
In stratified profiles, layers with k ratio > 10–100 relative to most permeable layer can be treated as impermeable; otherwise flow occurs in both with deflected lines at interface.
Anisotropic soils are transformed to equivalent isotropic using a = √(kmax/kmin) (Eq. 6-8); x-dimensions parallel to kmax direction are divided by a.

equations.description: Anisotropic to isotropic transformation factor: a = √(kmax/kmin), used to transform flow region dimensions for flow net construction.

sections.applicability: Applies when constructing flow nets for two-dimensional seepage analysis in isotropic, non-homogeneous, or anisotropic soil profiles.

sections.title: Interpreting Flow Nets
sections.summary: Explains how to extract quantitative results from a completed flow net, including calculation of volumetric flow rate using the shape factor Nf/Nd (Eq. 6-9), head loss per drop (Eq. 6-10), pore water pressures (Eq. 6-11), and hydraulic gradients. Introduces the shape factor concept and references Figure 6-5 for a worked example of discharge, uplift pressure, and gradient calculations.
sections.body:
Once drawn, flow nets can be used to calculate a number of properties including: seepage quantities, pore pressures, uplift forces, and hydraulic gradients. The volumetric flow rate through a flow net section can be calculated as:

q = k · hL · (Nf/Nd) · W  (6-9)

where: hL = the total differential head or head loss across the flow net, k = the isotropic hydraulic conductivity (use √(kmax·kmin) for transformed flow nets), Nf = the number of flow channels in the flow net, Nd = the total number of equipotential (head) drops in the flow net, and W = the width of the system perpendicular to the page, often taken as a unit width.

The ratio Nf / Nd from the flow net is sometimes referred to as the shape factor (SF). The shape factor incorporates the influence of geometry into the calculation of flow. Two flow nets with a different number of flow lines but the same value of SF will predict the same flow rates, total heads, and pore pressures.

The flow net divides the total head loss across the system into Nd equal head drops. The head loss associated with each head drop is:

∆hL = hL / Nd  (6-10)

where: ∆hL = the total differential head or head loss across one head drop, hL = the total differential head or head loss across the flow net, and Nd = the total number of head drops in the flow net.

The total head at any point within the flow net can be calculated by reference to the known total head at either the upstream or downstream boundary. The change in head from the boundary for any point is equal to the number of head drops from the boundary multiplied by ∆hL. By knowing the total head and elevation at a point of interest, the pore water pressure at any point can be calculated from the flow net as:

u = hp · γw = (ht - hz) · γw  (6-11)

where: hp = the pressure head at the point in question, ht = the total head at the point in question, hz = the elevation head at the point in question, and γw = the unit weight of water.

The hydraulic gradient can be calculated between any two points in the flow region by dividing the change in total head that occurs between two points by the distance over which the head loss occurs. When calculating gradients, it may be useful to subdivide flow net sections for more precision.

Figure 6-5 presents an example flow net with example calculations for discharge, uplift pressure, and hydraulic gradient.
key_points: Volumetric flow rate from flow net: q = k · hL · (Nf/Nd) · W (Eq. 6-9); for anisotropic transformed nets, k = √(kmax·kmin).
Shape factor SF = Nf/Nd incorporates geometry; nets with different Nf and Nd but equal SF give identical flow and pressure results.
Head loss per drop: ∆hL = hL/Nd (Eq. 6-10); total head at any point is found by counting drops from a known boundary.
Pore water pressure: u = (ht - hz) · γw (Eq. 6-11); requires knowing total head and elevation at the point.
Hydraulic gradient between two points = change in total head / distance; subdividing flow elements increases precision.
Flow nets yield seepage quantities, pore pressures, uplift forces, and hydraulic gradients from a single construction.

equations.description: Volumetric flow rate from flow net: q = k · hL · (Nf/Nd) · W, where Nf is number of flow channels, Nd is number of head drops, W is width.
Head loss per equipotential drop: ∆hL = hL / Nd, where hL is total head loss and Nd is total number of head drops.
Pore water pressure from total head: u = hp · γw = (ht − hz) · γw, using total head minus elevation head times unit weight of water.

sections.applicability: Applies when quantitative results (flow rates, pore pressures, uplift forces, hydraulic gradients) are needed from a completed two-dimensional flow net.

sections.title: Closed-Form Equations
sections.summary: Describes two closed-form solution methods for seepage beneath water-retaining structures: the method of fragments (Pavlovsky 1956, Harr 1977), which subdivides the flow region into standard-geometry fragments to determine shape factors and flow/pressure, and USACE blanket theory equations (USACE 2000), specifically designed for levee foundations with a low-permeability blanket over a high-permeability layer. Both can be implemented in spreadsheets.
sections.body:
The method of fragments and blanket theory are two closed-form solutions for calculation of seepage flow below water retaining structures. The method of fragments (Pavlovsky 1956, Harr 1977) subdivides the flow region into fragments of standard geometry. Based on the geometry, the SF for each fragment is determined along with the overall SF for the problem. The overall flow rate and pore pressures at particular points can be determined from the results. The blanket theory equations are based on the method of fragments and are particularly useful for seepage analyses of levees. These equations are specifically derived for a levee foundation condition consisting of a low-permeability 'blanket' layer overlying a high-permeability 'foundation' layer. The potential for soil heave occurring on the landside of the river can be readily assessed.

Both methods can be implemented in a spreadsheet application. For further information on the method of fragments and blanket theory equations, see Holtz et al. (2011) and Appendix B of USACE (1986), respectively.

Other common solutions have been developed for: (1) flow, heave potential, and exit gradients into excavations, (2) relief well design, and (3) dewatering well design. These specific solutions are presented in the later sections of this chapter.
key_points: Method of fragments divides the flow region into standard-geometry fragments; shape factors are computed for each to obtain overall flow rate and pore pressures.
Blanket theory equations (USACE 2000) are specifically suited for levee foundations with a low-permeability blanket over a high-permeability layer.
Blanket theory readily assesses landside heave potential; both methods are spreadsheet-implementable.
Additional closed-form solutions exist for excavation flow/heave/gradients, relief well design, and dewatering well design (covered later in Chapter 6).
References: method of fragments — Holtz et al. (2011); blanket theory — USACE (1986) Appendix B.
sections.applicability: Applies to seepage calculations beneath water-retaining structures, particularly levees with layered foundations, where spreadsheet-based closed-form solutions are preferred over numerical analysis.

sections.title: Numerical Seepage Analysis
sections.summary: Introduces numerical seepage analysis (primarily finite element analysis) as the appropriate tool for most seepage problems, offering user-friendly input, complex geometry handling, and rich graphical output. Notes that FEA can extend to 3D and transient/unsaturated conditions (beyond chapter scope), and emphasizes that graphical/analytical methods remain important for validating numerical models.
sections.body:
Numerical analysis, such as finite element or finite difference, is the appropriate tool for most seepage analysis problems. These methods are user-friendly and allow easy input of soil properties and complex geometric configurations, while providing rich graphical output. Numerical analyses also can be extended to three-dimensions and used to model unsaturated soils and transient flow conditions. However, those topics are beyond the scope of this chapter. The graphical and analytical methods discussed in Sections 6-2.4 and 6-2.5 provide an important means of validating numerical seepage models.

Finite element analysis (FEA) is the most common numerical approach used for seepage analysis, and this section is written from the perspective of FEA. Other numerical approaches, such as finite difference, will also provide suitable results but may use slightly different terminology.
key_points: Numerical analysis (FEA or finite difference) is appropriate for most seepage analysis problems due to flexibility with complex geometry and soil properties.
FEA can extend to 3D and transient/unsaturated conditions, but those topics are outside Chapter 6 scope.
Flow net and closed-form methods (Sections 6-2.4 and 6-2.5) serve as critical validation tools for numerical models.
FEA is the most common numerical approach; finite difference methods are also suitable with minor terminology differences.
sections.applicability: Applies when numerical seepage analysis is warranted for complex geometries, soil property variability, or when graphical methods are insufficient.

sections.title: General Concepts of Finite Element Seepage Analysis
sections.summary: Explains the fundamental concepts of FEA for seepage: subdivision of the flow domain into elements (triangles, quadrilaterals) connected at nodes, element matrices relating nodal heads to gradients and flow, assembly into a global matrix, and the nature of unknowns (head at interior/no-flow nodes; flow at specified-head boundaries). Describes linear and polynomial head variation within elements.
sections.body:
In finite element analysis, the flow region is divided into areas or volumes (referred to as elements) within which the flow of water can be easily defined. Elements are formed by connecting points in space (referred to as nodes) with lines. Two-dimensional elements are often three-node triangles or four-node quadrilaterals. Within each element the flow is defined with a system of equations that relate the hydraulic head at each node with the hydraulic gradient and flow within the element. These equations are described in an element matrix by linking the values of the common nodes. The equations (matrices) for each of the elements are assembled into a global matrix that represents a set of equations that define the flow through the entire system. For each node there is one equation and one unknown value for each node.

In the simplest form of element, the direction and magnitude of the hydraulic gradient throughout the element are constant. This results in the hydraulic head varying linearly along the element boundaries and within the elements themselves. In more advanced element types, the head varies according to a polynomial equation. Before solving the problem, the one unknown for each node is either (1) the total head at the node or (2) the total flow into and out of the system associated with the node. In general, nodes within the body of the problem and along no-flow boundaries have unknown head and total flow of zero (i.e., flow in equals flow out). At boundaries where flow enters the system, the flow is unknown but the head is generally specified.
key_points: Flow region is divided into elements (3-node triangles or 4-node quadrilaterals) connected at nodes.
Element matrices relate nodal hydraulic heads to gradient and flow; assembled into a global matrix for the entire system.
Each node has one equation and one unknown: either total head (interior/no-flow nodes) or nodal flow (specified-head boundaries).
Simplest elements use constant gradient and linear head variation; advanced elements use polynomial head variation.
At no-flow boundaries, head is unknown but flow is zero (flow in = flow out); at inflow/outflow boundaries, head is specified and flow is unknown.
sections.applicability: Applies when understanding or setting up a finite element seepage analysis model for a two-dimensional flow domain.

sections.title: Boundary Conditions
sections.summary: Describes the boundary conditions used in finite element seepage models, including constant head, constant pressure, no-flow (impermeable), nodal flow, infiltration, and unknown/variable conditions. Table 6-1 lists all common boundary condition types with descriptions and usage, and Table 6-2 shows their application to example seepage problems (impermeable dam, coffer dam, permeable dam/levee).
sections.body: Boundary conditions describe the head, pressure, and flow conditions at the boundaries of the model. Table 6-1 describes the most common boundary conditions used in basic finite element models. Table 6-2 illustrates the application of boundary conditions to finite element models.
key_points: Constant head BC: nodal heads are known and fixed; nodal flow is calculated; used for submerged boundaries and horizontal seepage exits.
Constant pressure BC: pressure head held constant (often = 0); used for seepage exits and internal drains.
No-flow BC: flow across boundary is zero; used for impermeable soil, rock, or structures.
Nodal flow BC: specifies inflow/outflow rate at a node; used for injection/extraction wells.
Infiltration BC: specifies inflow rate along an external boundary; used for rainwater or surface infiltration.
Unknown/variable BC: boundary alternates between no-flow and constant pressure based on analysis results; used for phreatic surface exit zones on dam/levee slopes.
sections.applicability: Applies when defining boundary conditions for finite element seepage models of dams, levees, cofferdams, and similar water-retaining or water-intersecting structures.

sections.title: Interpreting Output
sections.summary: Describes how to interpret the primary outputs of FEA seepage analysis—total hydraulic head and nodal flow at each node—and how post-processing yields hydraulic gradient, velocity, flow rate, pressure head, and uplift forces. Notes that commercial software typically automates these calculations via interpolation algorithms.
sections.body: The primary mathematical result of a finite element analysis are values of total hydraulic head and nodal flow for each node in the finite element mesh. By post-processing the total head and flow results from the FEA, the hydraulic gradient, hydraulic velocity, volumetric flow rate, pressure head, and uplift force along a boundary segment can be obtained. Most of the commercially available finite element seepage analysis software have post processors that will calculate these values through interpolation algorithms. Several of these interpretations are discussed below.
key_points: Primary FEA outputs are total hydraulic head and nodal flow at each mesh node.
Post-processing derives hydraulic gradient, velocity, volumetric flow rate, pressure head, and uplift forces.
Commercial FEA software typically includes post-processors using interpolation algorithms for these calculations.
sections.applicability: Applies when interpreting and post-processing results from finite element seepage analyses to obtain engineering design quantities.

sections.title: Pore Water Pressure
sections.summary: Describes how pore water pressure is calculated in FEA output using Equation 6-11, relating total head and elevation to pressure. Notes that commercial software typically generates contour maps of hydraulic pressure throughout the flow region for each node.
sections.body: The pore water pressure is calculated from the total head and the elevation using Equation 6-11. Generally, commercial software will calculate the hydraulic pressure for each node and provide a contour map of the pressure throughout the flow region.
key_points: Pore water pressure is calculated from Eq. 6-11: u = (ht − hz) · γw using nodal total head and elevation.
Commercial FEA software generates contour maps of hydraulic pressure throughout the flow region.

equations.description: Pore water pressure from FEA output: u = (ht − hz) · γw; referenced here in the context of post-processing nodal results.

sections.applicability: Applies when calculating pore water pressures from finite element seepage analysis results for stability, uplift, or design evaluations.

sections.title: Uplift Force
sections.summary: Explains how uplift force on a structure or soil mass is calculated from FEA results by integrating hydraulic pressures along specified boundary segments. Describes a simplified approach of plotting pressure contours, assigning representative areas to each contour interval, and summing the products of interval length and representative pressure.
sections.body: Uplift force due to hydraulic pressure on a structure or mass of soil is calculated by integrating the hydraulic pressures along a specified set of the boundary segments in the model. A simple estimate of the uplift force can be calculated by plotting the pore water pressure contours and assigning a representative area along the boundary segment to each contour interval. The total uplift force can be calculated by summing product of the interval length and the representative pressure for each interval.
key_points: Uplift force is calculated by integrating hydraulic pressures along specified boundary segments in the FEA model.
Simplified approach: plot pore pressure contours, assign representative area to each contour interval, sum (interval length × representative pressure).
This method applies to uplift on structures or soil masses subjected to seepage pressures.
sections.applicability: Applies when calculating uplift forces on structures or soil masses from finite element seepage analysis results.

sections.title: Hydraulic Gradients
sections.summary: Describes how hydraulic gradients are calculated in FEA seepage models, including interpolation methods for simple vs. higher-order elements, and warns about singularity effects near sharp corners where gradients can approach infinity as element size decreases. Guidance is given on appropriate gradient calculation distances near features like levee toes.
sections.body:
Hydraulic gradients are calculated for each element based on the hydraulic heads at the element nodes. Strictly speaking for simple elements, the hydraulic gradient in a given direction should be constant within each element. However, commercial software will often interpolate contours of hydraulic gradient based on the calculated head at each node. For higher order elements, the hydraulic gradient in a given direction may vary within the element. In these cases, the calculated gradients may be interpreted by plotting its variation within the flow region.

As a note of caution, the calculated hydraulic gradient will vary depending on the size of the element used near sharp corners in the flow region (often termed singularities). In this case, the calculated hydraulic gradients will increase as the element size decreases. As the element dimension approaches zero, the calculated hydraulic gradient may approach infinity. At these locations, the hydraulic gradients should be calculated over a distance consistent with the mechanisms of concern and known ground conditions. For example, the hydraulic gradient at the toe of a levee resting on a blanket layer of low k soil should be calculated across the thickness of the blanket.
key_points: Hydraulic gradients are computed from nodal hydraulic heads; constant within simple elements, variable within higher-order elements.
Commercial software often interpolates gradient contours from nodal head values.
Near singularities (sharp corners), computed gradients increase as element size decreases and may approach infinity at zero element dimension.
At singularities, gradients should be evaluated over a distance consistent with the failure mechanism and ground conditions (e.g., blanket layer thickness at levee toe).
sections.applicability: Applies when interpreting hydraulic gradient outputs from FEA seepage models, especially near geometric singularities.

sections.title: Discharge Velocity
sections.summary: States that discharge velocity in FEA seepage models is computed from the element hydraulic gradient and assigned hydraulic conductivity using Darcy's law (Equation 6-5). This is a brief procedural note on how FEA post-processing derives velocity from gradient and k values.
sections.body: Discharge velocity is calculated from the hydraulic gradient and the hydraulic conductivity assigned to the element using Equation 6-5.
key_points: Discharge velocity = hydraulic gradient × hydraulic conductivity (Darcy's law, Eq. 6-5).
Both the gradient and k value are element-specific in FEA models.

equations.description: Darcy's law: discharge velocity calculated from hydraulic gradient and hydraulic conductivity assigned to the element.

sections.applicability: Applies when computing discharge velocity for individual elements in FEA seepage analyses.

sections.title: Seepage Flow Volume
sections.summary: Explains how seepage flow volumes are calculated in FEA models using Darcy's law (Eq. 6-3). Flow rates across model boundaries are determined from the perpendicular hydraulic gradient component, element hydraulic conductivity, and boundary area. Flow across interior lines is computed similarly using intersected element areas.
sections.body: Seepage volumes are calculated for elements using Darcy's law (Equation 6-3). For flow across a model boundary, the flow rate through each element is calculated, using the vector component of hydraulic gradient perpendicular to the boundary, the hydraulic conductivity assigned to the element, and the area of the element boundary along the model boundary. The flow rate across a portion of an FEA model can be assessed by calculating the flow across a line using a similar methodology applied to the area associated with the elements intersected by the line.
key_points: Seepage flow volumes are computed element-by-element using Darcy's law (Eq. 6-3).
Boundary flow rates use the perpendicular gradient component, element k, and boundary face area.
Flow across any interior cross-section can be evaluated by summing contributions from all elements intersected by a defined line.

equations.description: Darcy's law used to calculate seepage flow volume for elements and across model boundaries.

sections.applicability: Applies when calculating seepage flow volumes or rates across boundaries and interior cross-sections in FEA seepage models.

sections.title: Hydraulic Conductivity (Coefficient of Permeability)
sections.summary: Introduces hydraulic conductivity as one of the most variable soil properties, ranging over 8 orders of magnitude (10⁻⁸ cm/sec for high-plasticity clay to >1 cm/sec for open-graded gravel). Clarifies terminology distinctions between hydraulic conductivity, coefficient of permeability, and permeability, and outlines three assessment strategies: laboratory testing, field testing, and empirical correlations.
sections.body:
One of the most varied soil properties in geotechnical engineering is hydraulic conductivity, which can be defined as the discharge velocity of water through a unit area under a unit hydraulic gradient. Common hydraulic conductivity values can range from less 10-8 cm/sec for high plasticity clay to in excess of 1 cm/sec for open graded gravels; a range of over 8 orders of magnitude. Small changes in soil gradation, especially changes in the fines content, can result in significant variation in hydraulic conductivity.

Terminology regarding hydraulic conductivity is varied across the profession. The term coefficient of permeability is used as a synonym for hydraulic conductivity in literature. The practicing geotechnical community commonly uses the term "permeability" interchangeably with hydraulic conductivity. However, this is technically incorrect as permeability is a property of the porous media alone and does not consider the viscosity of the permeant fluid. Hydraulic conductivity is the preferred term, but both hydraulic conductivity and permeability are used in this manual.

Hydraulic conductivity is most often required for in situ soil conditions. Hydraulic conductivity can be assessed for these conditions by several strategies: 1) laboratory testing, 2) field testing, and 3) empirical correlations including equations, charts, and tables. Each of these are discussed in the following subsections.
key_points: Hydraulic conductivity ranges over 8 orders of magnitude: ~10⁻⁸ cm/sec (high-plasticity clay) to >1 cm/sec (open-graded gravel).
Small changes in gradation, especially fines content, can cause large changes in k.
'Permeability' and 'hydraulic conductivity' are used interchangeably in practice, but technically permeability is a porous media property independent of fluid viscosity.
Three assessment approaches: laboratory testing, field testing, and empirical correlations.
Hydraulic conductivity is the preferred term in this manual, though both terms are used.
sections.applicability: Applies as an introduction to hydraulic conductivity assessment for any geotechnical seepage or flow analysis.

sections.title: Laboratory Testing
sections.summary: Discusses laboratory permeability testing on intact and reconstituted samples, referencing Section 3-2.7 for procedures. Highlights key limitations: small sample size, typically measuring vertical k, inability to capture deposit-scale anisotropy or layering, and impossibility of intact sampling of coarse-grained soils. Recommends lab testing primarily for reconstituted samples (fills, cutoff walls, pond liners, filters).
sections.body: Laboratory tests can be performed on intact samples or reconstituted samples. Details of laboratory testing procedures are presented in Section 3-2.7. While laboratory tests can measure the hydraulic conductivity of a wide range of soils, the limitations of laboratory testing must be acknowledged. First, laboratory tests use a small sample of soil or rock and usually test the vertical permeability because the samples are obtained from boreholes. As a result, laboratory test results may not be representative of the large-scale properties of a soil deposit if the layering and structure of the deposit is not considered. Natural soils usually exhibit anisotropy with the horizontal permeability being larger than the vertical. Thus, laboratory tests are likely to result in lower values than are appropriate for many types of analyses. Finally, intact samples of coarse-grained soils cannot be obtained using normal sampling procedures. Laboratory tests on reconstituted specimens of these materials are likely no more reliable than correlations. With the above in mind, laboratory permeability testing is most appropriately reserved for reconstituted samples for applications such as fill materials, cutoff wall backfills, pond liners, and filter materials.
key_points: Lab tests on intact or reconstituted samples; procedures per Section 3-2.7.
Lab tests measure vertical k (borehole samples) — may underestimate horizontal k for anisotropic natural soils.
Small sample size means results may not represent deposit-scale behavior if layering is not considered.
Intact sampling of coarse-grained soils is not feasible; reconstituted lab tests are no more reliable than empirical correlations.
Lab testing is best suited for reconstituted samples: fill materials, cutoff wall backfills, pond liners, and filter materials.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting laboratory permeability testing for natural or engineered soil materials, particularly for evaluating its limitations versus other methods.

sections.title: Field Testing
sections.summary: Identifies two classes of field hydraulic conductivity testing — borehole tests and pumping tests — with procedures referenced in Chapter 2. Borehole tests characterize soil near the borehole; pumping tests provide broader areal permeability characteristics over a larger zone of influence.
sections.body: Two classes of field hydraulic conductivity testing are borehole tests and field pumping tests. Details of field testing procedures are presented in Chapter 2. Borehole tests are effective in measuring the permeability of the soil in the general area of the borehole. To measure permeability characteristics over a broader area, a pumping test can be performed.
key_points: Two field test types: borehole tests (local k) and pumping tests (areal average k).
Borehole tests measure permeability in the vicinity of the borehole only.
Pumping tests characterize hydraulic conductivity over a broader area.
Detailed procedures are in Chapter 2.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting field testing methods to measure in situ hydraulic conductivity at different spatial scales.

sections.title: Empirical Relationships for Hydraulic Conductivity
sections.summary: Reviews empirical and semi-empirical methods for estimating hydraulic conductivity from grain-size and gradation data. Covers Figure 6-6 (k vs. soil classification), Table 6-3 (horizontal k for natural soils and rock, USBR), Table 6-4 (vertical k for compacted embankment soils, USBR), Table 6-5 (grain-size correlations), the general Eq. 6-12 power-law form, the Kozeny-Carman Eq. 6-13, the void-ratio ratio Eq. 6-14, and Figure 6-7 (k vs. fines content).
sections.body:
Numerous empirical and semi-empirical relationships have been developed for correlating hydraulic conductivity with other soil properties (predominantly grain size and gradation). The simplest of these relationships relate soil type to typical values of ranges of k. Figure 6-6 correlates k with soil classification types for various unit systems.

The United States Bureau of Reclamation (USBR 2014) has determined typical values for the horizontal hydraulic conductivity of natural soil and rock deposits based on field testing as indicated in Table 6-3 and the vertical hydraulic conductivity of embankment fill materials based on laboratory testing as summarized in Table 6-4.

The size of the pore spaces is one of the most important factors controlling the hydraulic conductivity of a soil, especially for coarse-grained materials. The effective diameter or effective grain size (Dα) is the grain size that has the primary influence on the average pore size of the soil. In terms of the effects on hydraulic conductivity, the α refers to a particular percent passing on the grain-size distribution and typically has been assigned a value of 5, 10, 15, or 20. In other words, the effects of pore size on hydraulic conductivity has been found to correlate best with particle diameters corresponding to the 5 to 20% passing size. Correlations that relate hydraulic conductivity to an effective grain size or grain-size distribution can be expressed as (Kenney et al. 1984):

k = βα × Dα^x   (6-12)

where:
k = hydraulic conductivity,
βα = empirical or semi-empirical coefficient,
Dα = effective grain size,
α = percent passing corresponding to effective grain size, and
x = exponent - theoretically equal to 2 and empirically slightly above 2.

Most of the published correlations for the hydraulic conductivity of coarse-grained soils can be expressed in terms of Equation 6-12. These correlations are summarized in Table 6-5. Some of the relationships also account for the effect of void ratio on k.

The Kozeny-Carman equation (Carrier 2003) can be used to account for the effect of the entire grain-size distribution and the particle shape:

k = 1.99×10^-2 × [e^3/(1+e)] / [S × Σ(fi/(Dli^0.404 × Dsi^0.596)) / 100%]^2   (6-13)

where:
k = hydraulic conductivity (cm/sec),
fi = fraction of particles (by mass) between two adjacent sieve sizes,
Dli = the particle size of the coarser sieve (mm),
Dsi = the particle size of the finer sieve (mm),
S = surface area factor ranging from 6 for spheres to 8.5 for angular particles, and
e = void ratio.

For a given soil, the ratio of hydraulic conductivities under two different void ratios can be considered by (Kozeny 1927):

k1/k2 = [e1^3/(1+e1)] / [e2^3/(1+e2)]   (6-14)

where:
k1 = hydraulic conductivity for void ratio, e1, and
k2 = hydraulic conductivity for void ratio, e2.

For fine-grained soils, the hydraulic conductivity would be expected to decrease as liquid limit, plasticity index, or fines content increase. Figure 6-7 shows that hydraulic conductivity decreases as the fine content (percent passing the No. 200 sieve) increases. For a given fines content, the range of kv is 2.5 to 3 orders of magnitude with sandy and silty soils having higher kv than clayey soils.
key_points: Figure 6-6 provides k ranges by soil classification type across multiple unit systems.
USBR Table 6-3 gives horizontal k for natural soils and rock; Table 6-4 gives vertical k for compacted embankment materials.
Eq. 6-12: k = βα·Dα^x — general power-law correlation of k to effective grain size (D5 to D20); x ≈ 2 theoretically.
Table 6-5 summarizes published grain-size k correlations (Hazen, Slichter, Chapuis, Carrier, Sherard, Kenney), many incorporating void ratio.
Eq. 6-13 (Kozeny-Carman): accounts for full grain-size distribution and particle shape via surface area factor S (6 for spheres, 8.5 for angular).
Eq. 6-14 (Kozeny): relates k at two different void ratios; useful for compaction or consolidation effects.
Figure 6-7: k decreases with increasing fines content; at a given fines content, kv spans 2.5–3 orders of magnitude.

equations.description: General power-law correlation of hydraulic conductivity to effective grain size: k = βα·Dα^x, where x ≈ 2 theoretically and βα is an empirical coefficient.
Kozeny-Carman equation: estimates hydraulic conductivity accounting for full grain-size distribution, particle shape (surface area factor S), and void ratio e.
Kozeny (1927) void-ratio correction: ratio of hydraulic conductivities at two void ratios, k1/k2 = [e1^3/(1+e1)] / [e2^3/(1+e2)].

figures: Figure 6-6 — Variation of Hydraulic Conductivity with Soil Type for Various Unit Systems (after Freeze and Cherry 1979)
Figure 6-7 — Variation of Hydraulic Conductivity with Fines Content (after California Department of Water Resources 2013)
tables: Table 6-3 — Typical Ranges of Horizontal Hydraulic Conductivity for Natural Soil and Unfractured Rock Deposits (after USBR 2014)
Table 6-4 — Typical Range of Vertical Hydraulic Conductivity for Compacted Soil in Embankments (after USBR 2014)
Table 6-5 — Estimating Hydraulic Conductivity based on Effective Grain Size
sections.applicability: Applies when estimating hydraulic conductivity using empirical methods based on soil classification, grain size, gradation, or void ratio for coarse- or fine-grained soils.

sections.title: Anisotropy
sections.summary: Introduces the concept of hydraulic conductivity anisotropy in soils. Notes that natural soils typically exhibit horizontal k greater than vertical k due to depositional layering, but mentions that vertical cracks can create exceptions where vertical k exceeds horizontal k. Section continues beyond this chunk.
sections.body: More often than not soils exhibit anisotropy with respect to hydraulic conductivity. In natural soils this is usually a consequence of depositional layering of the soil and results in horizontal hydraulic conductivity greater than in the vertical direction. However, in some cases, often related to the formation and filling of vertical cracks, the vertical [section continues].
key_points: Most natural soils exhibit hydraulic conductivity anisotropy due to depositional layering.
Horizontal k typically exceeds vertical k in naturally deposited soils.
Vertical cracking can create conditions where vertical k exceeds horizontal k.
sections.applicability: Applies when assessing directional differences in hydraulic conductivity for natural or engineered soil deposits.

sections.title: Internal Erosion
sections.summary: Introduces internal erosion as a leading cause of dam failures (~50%), defines the term, and explains the evolution of nomenclature culminating in the 2014 ICOLD system. Internal erosion encompasses erosion of particles by seeping water through soil/rock voids or preferential flow paths such as cracks. Covers four main sub-mechanisms: heave, erosion and stoping, and internal instability.
sections.body:
About half of dam failures and accidents can be attributed to internal erosion through the foundation and/or through the embankment or along a penetration through the embankment (e.g., Foster et al. 2000). Internal erosion is a generic term that describes erosion of particles caused by water seeping through a body of soil or rock. The water may be seeping through the interstitial voids of a soil or rock mass, or may be flowing along pathways of preferential flow (cracks or other defects).

Terminology describing the various mechanisms of internal erosion has evolved in recent years as understanding of the mechanisms of erosion have developed. Nomenclature for these mechanisms has been and continues to be inconsistent in practice and in the literature due to this rapid evolution of understanding and nomenclature. For example, the terms "piping" and "seepage-related erosion" have been used as generic terms for internal erosion, and the term "internal erosion" has been used to denote a specific internal erosion mechanism.

In 2014, the International Commission on Large Dams (ICOLD) adopted a system of nomenclature describing the various mechanisms of internal erosion. The ICOLD nomenclature is summarized in the following sections along with additions to the nomenclature where necessary.
key_points: About 50% of dam failures and accidents are attributed to internal erosion through foundation, embankment, or along penetrations.
Internal erosion refers to erosion of particles caused by seeping water moving through soil/rock voids or preferential flow paths (cracks, defects).
Nomenclature has been inconsistent historically; 'piping' and 'seepage-related erosion' were used generically.
In 2014, ICOLD adopted a standardized nomenclature for the various mechanisms of internal erosion, used as the basis for this section.
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating internal erosion risk in dams, levees, embankments, and their foundations.

sections.title: Heave
sections.summary: Describes two types of heave as internal erosion mechanisms: effective stress heave (quick condition), where high hydraulic gradients lift coarse-grained soil at an unprotected exit; and total stress heave (blowout), where high pore pressure in an underlying aquifer uplifts a low-permeability layer. Both can occur at deep excavations and hydraulic structures on sand or clay underlain by aquifers.
sections.body:
Effective stress heave (a.k.a., quick condition) is the uplift of a mass of coarse-grained soil due to a high hydraulic gradient acting on soil particles at an unprotected exit. Seepage forces developed through viscous drag tend to lift the soil mass, resulting in uplift or a quick condition, as illustrated in Figure 6-8a.

Coarse-grained soils with high vertical hydraulic exit gradients are susceptible to effective stress heave. These gradients may occur at the base of deep excavations into sand and at the toe of hydraulic structures founded on sand.

Total stress heave (a.k.a., blowout) is the uplift of a mass of low-permeability soil due to high hydraulic pressure in an underlying aquifer as shown in Figure 6-8b. When the pressure beneath a layer with low hydraulic conductivity exceeds the total weight of the layer, uplift occurs and often results in cracking of the upper layer. Total stress heave occurs in fine-grained soils with underlying aquifers, such as deep excavations into clay and fine-grained blankets.
key_points: Effective stress heave (quick condition): uplift of coarse-grained soil mass due to high vertical hydraulic exit gradient via seepage-induced viscous drag.
Susceptible locations for effective stress heave: base of deep excavations into sand and toes of hydraulic structures on sand.
Total stress heave (blowout): uplift of low-permeability layer when underlying aquifer pressure exceeds total overburden weight, often causing cracking.
Total stress heave occurs in fine-grained soils overlying artesian aquifers, e.g., deep excavations into clay or fine-grained blankets.
sections.applicability: Applies when assessing uplift risk at excavations, hydraulic structures, or embankments founded on or underlain by pressurized aquifers.

sections.title: Erosion and Stoping
sections.summary: Defines and distinguishes five internal erosion mechanisms involving particle removal and void propagation: backward erosion piping (classical piping with stable roof), general backward erosion (progressive sloughing without roof), stoping (vertical void collapse as sinkholes), concentrated leak erosion (shear along cracks/conduit gaps), and contact erosion (shear at permeable/erodible soil contacts). Each has distinct susceptible conditions and morphology.
sections.body:
Backward erosion piping (a.k.a., classical piping) is the successive removal of soil particles at an unprotected exit resulting in the formation of an open pathway or pipe that progresses toward the source of the seepage. A stable roof prevents collapse of the pipe and allows its progression, as illustrated in Figure 6-9a. The toes of dams and levees are especially susceptible to backward erosion piping, along with unprotected exits, such the ground surface, internal voids or pathways, or defects in a conduit or outlet.

General backward erosion (a.k.a., progressive sloughing or internal migration) is the successive removal of soil particles at an unprotected exit resulting in progressive sloughing of a slope. This type of erosion initiates similar to backward erosion piping, but the lack of a "roof" prevents the progression of a pipe (Figure 6-9b). Slopes and embankments consisting of coarse-grained soils with high seepage flows are susceptible to general backward erosion.

Stoping (a.k.a., sinkhole) is the near-vertical progression of a void caused by successive collapse into a cavity as shown in Figure 6-9c. The cavity is often the result of another internal erosion mechanism. Stopes often manifest as sinkholes at the ground surface and occur in embankments with moderate to low cohesive strength.

Concentrated leak erosion (a.k.a., scour) is erosion that occurs along a concentrated flow path and is caused by shear forces imposed by the flowing water (Figure 6-9d). Concentrated leaks may be cracks within the soil or rock, gaps between soil and a conduit or structure, or other pathways of low flow-resistance capable of carrying eroded soil particles. Conditions that are susceptible to concentrated leak erosion include cohesive embankments, outlet pipes and structures in embankments, and dam and levee fill placed along steep rock abutments.

Contact erosion (a.k.a., scour) is erosion that occurs along a contact between a highly permeable material and an erodible soil. Contact erosion is caused by shear forces imposed by high seepage velocities in the highly permeable material as illustrated in Figure 6-9e. The contacts between erodible soil and open-graded gravel or open joints in bedrock are locations susceptible to this type of erosion.
key_points: Backward erosion piping (classical piping): pipe progresses toward seepage source at unprotected exit; requires a stable roof; toes of dams and levees are highly susceptible.
General backward erosion (progressive sloughing): similar to backward erosion piping but lacks a stable roof, so a pipe cannot form; affects coarse-grained slopes with high seepage.
Stoping (sinkhole): near-vertical void progression by successive collapse into a cavity, often initiated by another erosion mechanism; manifests as surface sinkholes.
Concentrated leak erosion (scour): shear-driven erosion along cracks, conduit gaps, or low-resistance flow paths; common in cohesive embankments and along rock abutments.
Contact erosion (scour): shear-driven erosion at the contact between highly permeable material (e.g., open-graded gravel, jointed rock) and an erodible soil due to high seepage velocities.
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating internal erosion failure modes in dams, levees, embankments, conduits, and rock-fill contacts under seepage conditions.

sections.title: Internal Instability
sections.summary: Describes internal instability, where fine particles erode from within a coarse-grained skeleton under seepage. Distinguishes suffusion (coarse particles in contact; no volume change) from suffosion (coarse particles not in contact; volume change possible). Relevant for gap-graded or broadly graded soils prone to selective particle migration under hydraulic gradients.
sections.body: Soils can be internally unstable such that fine-grained particles erode from within a framework or "skeleton" of coarse-grained particles as illustrated in Figure 6-10. The process is called suffusion if the coarse-grained particles are in contact with each other before erosion. Thus, no volume change results from suffusion. The process is called suffosion if the coarse-grained particles are not in contact with each other before erosion.
key_points: Internal instability: fine particles migrate out of a coarse-grained skeleton under seepage forces.
Suffusion: coarse particles are in contact before erosion — fine particle loss causes no volume change in the soil matrix.
Suffosion: coarse particles are NOT in contact before erosion — fine particle loss can result in volume change and settlement.
Internally unstable soils are typically gap-graded or broadly graded materials susceptible to selective particle migration.
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating gap-graded or broadly graded soils in embankments, filters, or foundations for susceptibility to internal particle migration.

sections.title: Seepage and Internal Erosion Mitigation Methods
sections.summary: Top-level container section covering the full range of seepage and internal erosion mitigation methods for earthen dams, levees, excavations, and other structures subject to differential water pressure. Introduces the three main problem categories (excess flow, high pore pressure, internal erosion) and three general mitigation strategies (barriers, controlled drainage, filtration).
key_points: Seepage problems fall into three categories: excess volumetric flow rate, high pore water pressures, and internal erosion potential.
Three general mitigation strategies: seepage barriers, controlled drainage, and filtration.
Seepage severity can be evaluated using Table 6-8 (q/hL/W thresholds) to determine if remediation is needed.
Blocking seepage can increase pressures and gradients elsewhere; engineers must assess resulting stability and internal erosion risk.
Controlled drainage reduces pore pressures but typically increases volumetric flow rate.
Sand and gravel filters are the most reliable long-term solution to halt internal erosion progression.
sections.applicability: Applies whenever seepage through or beneath earthen embankments, dams, levees, or excavations must be evaluated or mitigated.

sections.title: Problems and General Strategies
sections.summary: Describes the three categories of seepage problems (excess flow rate, high pore water pressures, internal erosion potential) and the three corresponding mitigation strategies (seepage barriers, controlled drainage, filtration). Introduces Table 6-8 for evaluating seepage severity and determining whether remediation is required.
sections.body:
Seepage occurs through all earthen dam and levee embankments and their foundations, into excavations below the water table, and below other structures subjected to differential water pressure conditions. In many cases, the quantity of seepage is such that it poses no adverse consequences or risk to the structure. However, if seepage is excessive or the pressures and forces associated with the seepage are too great, mitigation of the seepage issues may be required. Problems associated with seepage can be classified into three categories:
a. Excess volumetric flow rate of seepage
Undesirable consequences of excess flow include the loss of valuable water from a reservoir, flooded or soft ground in excavations, and wet ground conditions below a dam or levee that prevent activities or usage of the land.
b. High pore water pressures
High pore water pressures can result in unacceptable uplift forces beneath or within dams and levees that lead to instability with respect to sliding or overturning. Excessive water pressure forces can also act on buildings, retaining walls, and other appurtenant structures.
c. Internal erosion potential
Some seepage conditions may create a condition where internal erosion is likely through one of the mechanisms described in Section 6-4. Internal erosion problems are often tied to high pore water pressures. Assessment of internal erosion potential should be paired with an evaluation of the severity of seepage. Table 6-8 provides a means to evaluate seepage severity and assess if further investigation is required. This approach recognizes that the flow rate must be sufficiently high for problematic internal erosion to occur.
If one or more of the problems described above must be mitigated, the mitigation typically employs one of three general strategies:
a. Seepage barriers
This strategy consists of constructing an element that either directly blocks the seepage pathway or lengthens the seepage pathway. Blocking seepage can result in increased hydraulic pressures and hydraulic gradients in some locations within an embankment or foundation. When methods to block seepage are used, the engineer must assess whether the resulting pressures and gradients will be detrimental to structural stability and the internal erosion potential.
b. Providing controlled drainage
In locations where high pore water pressures result in either high hydraulic gradients or uplift forces, the pressures can be reduced by providing a controlled drainage system. The control in such a system involves assuring that the water can be drained without causing internal erosion or resulting in excessive water losses. Controlled drainage typically increases the volumetric flow rate.
c. Providing Filtration
In locations where there is potential for internal erosion, the progression of erosion can be halted by providing adequate filtration of the eroding soil particles. The most reliable and long-lasting filters are constructed using sands and gravels graded to specifications that provide both soil particle retention and adequate seepage flow capacity.
key_points: Three seepage problem categories: excess flow, high pore pressures, and internal erosion potential.
Table 6-8 classifies seepage severity from Negligible to Heavy using q/hL/W (cfs per ft of head per ft of levee).
Heavy seepage (q/hL/W > 2.2×10⁻⁴) requires remediation; negligible (<2.2×10⁻⁵) does not.
Seepage barriers can increase hydraulic gradients elsewhere — must be assessed for stability and erosion risk.
Controlled drainage reduces pressures but increases flow rate.
Sand/gravel filters graded to retain base soil particles are the most reliable filtration approach.
sections.applicability: Applies to all projects involving seepage through or beneath embankments, dams, levees, and excavations where remediation may be required.

sections.title: Seepage Barriers
sections.summary: Container section covering the full range of seepage barrier options, including vertical cutoff walls, upstream seepage blankets, downstream seepage berms, cutoff trenches, foundation grouting, and liners. These methods either block the flow path or lengthen it to reduce seepage volume and hydraulic gradients.
sections.body: Seepage barriers include a range of options for (1) blocking flow through a high-permeability layer of soil or rock or (2) extending the seepage pathway to reduce seepage volume and hydraulic gradients.
key_points: Seepage barriers either directly block flow or lengthen the seepage path to reduce gradients and volumes.
Options include vertical cutoff walls, upstream blankets, downstream berms, cutoff trenches, foundation grouting, and liners.
Selection depends on site geometry, soil/rock conditions, construction access, and acceptable risk.
sections.applicability: Applies when the primary mitigation strategy is to reduce seepage volume or hydraulic gradients by blocking or extending the seepage pathway.

sections.title: Vertical Barriers
sections.summary: Describes vertical seepage cutoff walls used to block seepage through permeable embankments, foundations, or aquifers. Covers all major construction methods (steel sheet piles, vinyl sheet piles, continuous slurry trench, element slurry wall, vertical membrane, deep mixing, jet grout) and backfill types (SB, CB, SCB, soil cement, plastic concrete, conventional concrete) with their characteristics and limitations.
sections.body:
Vertical barriers or seepage cutoff walls are zones with low hydraulic conductivity that are constructed (1) through permeable dam and levee embankments, (2) through dam and levee foundations with permeable layers, (3) surrounding excavations below the ground water table, or (4) blocking aquifers to prevent the spread of groundwater contamination. Vertical barriers are generally classified based on the excavation or construction method and the backfill type.
The various construction methods, their application, characteristics, and requirements are summarized in Table 6-9. Continuous slurry trenches are generally backfilled using one of three material types: Soil-Bentonite (SB) backfill, Cement-Bentonite (CB) backfill, and Soil-Cement-Bentonite (SCB) backfill. Element slurry walls are generally backfilled with concrete or plastic concrete using the Tremie method that fills the element from the bottom up while displacing the slurry. The characteristics of vertical barrier backfill materials are presented in Table 6-10.
key_points: Vertical cutoff walls are classified by construction method and backfill type; see Table 6-9 for method descriptions and Table 6-10 for backfill characteristics.
Steel and vinyl sheet piles rely on interlock integrity; corrosion (steel) and chemical stability (vinyl) must be assessed.
Continuous slurry trenches are susceptible to 'windows' from partial wall collapse or sand settling.
Element slurry walls (using clamshell or hydrocutter) allow excavation into most soils and rock with better joint control.
Deep mixing adjusts strength and permeability via slurry dosing; limited to soil and very soft rock.
Jet grout walls can seal irregular surfaces but carry high hydrofracture risk in embankments and are typically more expensive.
SB backfill is low-strength and highly compressible; CB and SCB are less prone to consolidation; conventional concrete is stiffest but may cause stress concentrations.
sections.applicability: Applies when a low-hydraulic-conductivity vertical barrier is needed through permeable embankments, foundations, or to contain groundwater contamination.

sections.title: Required Penetration for Cutoff Walls in Supported Excavations
sections.summary: Provides design guidance for determining the required embedment depth of vertical cutoff walls to prevent base heave (quick condition or blowout) in supported excavations. References Figures 6-11 through 6-13 (based on Marsland 1953) for homogeneous isotropic sand, stratified sand, and sand with fine-grained layers. Recommends a factor of safety of 1.5 to 2 against effective stress heave.
sections.body:
To prevent instability of the base of supported excavations due to heave (i.e., quick condition or blowout), the vertical cutoffs must extend deep enough to reduce hydraulic gradients or uplift pressures to acceptable levels. The first option to consider for embedment is to extend the cutoff to a low-permeability layer having considerable thickness. However, this is not always feasible.
In uniform pervious sands, critical hydraulic gradients may develop at the base of the excavation. The required wall penetration to provide a factor of safety against effective stress heave (quick condition) and piping in homogenous, isotropic sands can be calculated using Figure 6-11. For homogenous, anisotropic sands, the penetration depth can be reduced by the transformation factor, a (see Section 6-2.4.1 Equation 6-8). For clean sand, exit gradients greater than about 0.5 to 0.75 will cause unstable conditions for men and equipment operating on the subgrade. To avoid instability, provide sheeting penetration for a safety factor of 1.5 to 2 against effective stress heave as calculated in Figure 6-8.
In layered sands, variation in permeability results in a change of seepage conditions from that assumed in Figure 6-11. Figure 6-12 presents guidance for situations with layered sands. In layered soils with layers of very fine sand, silty or clayey sand, or silt and clay, the risk of bottom heave (total stress heave) must be considered. Figure 6-13 presents guidance for avoiding bottom heave in excavations.
