Alternatively, the conditions can be assessed using flow nets or finite element analyses, and Figure 6-11 through Figure 6-13 can be used to confirm the results.
The relationships presented in Figure 6-11 through Figure 6-13 were developed based on the results of laboratory modeling performed by Marsland (1953). The results were reported for loose and dense sands. Loose sands were placed 'with a water jet' while the dense sands were placed 'with an electrically vibrated' hammer. No relative densities were reported although porosities of 42 percent and 37 to 38 percent were reported for the loose and dense sands, respectively.
key_points: Cutoff walls must penetrate deep enough to prevent quick condition or blowout at the excavation base.
Figure 6-11 gives required penetration for homogeneous isotropic sand; use the transformation factor for anisotropic sands.
Exit gradients > 0.5–0.75 in clean sand cause unstable conditions; design for FS = 1.5 to 2 against effective stress heave.
Figure 6-12 provides corrections for stratified sands; Figure 6-13 addresses sand with fine-grained layers (total stress heave risk).
Flow nets or finite element analyses can be used as alternatives, with Figures 6-11 to 6-13 for verification.
Figures based on Marsland (1953) laboratory models; loose sand porosity ~42%, dense sand ~37–38%.
sections.applicability: Applies when designing the required embedment depth of vertical cutoff walls supporting excavations in pervious sands to prevent base heave or piping.

sections.title: Seepage Blankets and Berms
sections.summary: Covers upstream seepage blankets and downstream seepage berms as passive seepage control measures for dams and levees. Upstream blankets extend the seepage path to reduce flow and exit gradients. Downstream berms (impermeable, permeable, or composite) resist uplift pressures from low-permeability blanket layers. Design concerns include differential settlement, berm length, drainage capacity, and filter compatibility.
sections.body:
Upstream seepage blankets are constructed upstream of a dam or levee to increase the seepage pathway as depicted in Figure 6-14a. Upstream blankets are constructed of compacted fill with low hydraulic conductivity or a geomembrane protected with a coarse-grained soil cover. The increased seepage pathway will tend to decrease the amount of seepage, decrease uplift pressures below the dam or levee, and decrease exit gradients. The primary design concern of seepage blankets is providing a uniform foundation for the blanket. Differential settlement of the blanket under reservoir loading can result in tearing or cracking of the blanket and concentrated leakage, decreasing the effectiveness of the blanket.
Downstream seepage berms are designed to prevent excessive hydraulic pressures on the downstream side of a small dam or levee. Often these pressures are the result of a low hydraulic conductivity soil layer (blanket layer) that blocks the exit of seepage water. Seepage berms are usually constructed using one of three designs: (1) an impermeable berm, (2) a permeable berm, or (3) a composite berm.
The concept of an impermeable berm used to resist uplift pressures on a low-permeability blanket layer is presented in Figure 6-14b. The berm is constructed of generally low-permeability soils and is designed to increase the weight of the blanket layer thereby resisting total-stress heave. For blanket layers that allow some seepage, the impermeable berm will increase the resistance to seepage flow through the blanket layer, resulting in higher pressures below the levee and downstream toe. This also requires the berm to extend long distances from the levee in order to produce low uplift pressures beyond the berm.
A permeable seepage berm is illustrated in Figure 6-14c. The permeable berm is constructed of permeable materials (generally sand) that increase the total weight on the blanket without significantly increasing seepage resistance. Where the blanket layer is sufficiently permeable to allow seepage on the landside, permeable berms can be much shorter than impermeable berms. A disadvantage of this berm type is that appropriate high-permeability soils can be very expensive in some locales.
A composite seepage berm consists of an upper layer of undifferentiated fill underlain by a drain and filter layer (see Figure 6-14d). Thus, the berm acts similar to the permeable berm but is less expensive because less of the filter material is required. The drainage layer must be designed with adequate flow capacity to prevent the buildup of water pressure in the layer. In some cases, pipes have been included in the drainage layer to increase flow capacity. However, such pipes increase the amount of maintenance needed for the berm.
key_points: Upstream blankets extend the seepage path, reducing flow rate, uplift pressures, and exit gradients downstream.
Differential settlement is the primary design concern for upstream blankets — cracking or tearing concentrates leakage.
Three downstream berm types: impermeable (adds weight, requires long extent), permeable (shorter but costly material), and composite (combines fill with a drainage layer).
Impermeable berms can increase subsurface pressures if the blanket layer is not fully impermeable.
Composite berms are cost-effective but require careful drain flow capacity design; embedded pipes increase maintenance.
All downstream berm designs must address filter compatibility at the drainage layer interface.
sections.applicability: Applies to small dams and levees where upstream or downstream passive measures are needed to control seepage volume, uplift pressures, and exit gradients.

sections.title: Other Types of Seepage Barriers
sections.summary: Container section grouping three additional seepage barrier types: cutoff trenches (used in original dam/levee construction), foundation grouting (for reducing hydraulic conductivity of fractured bedrock), and liners (for ponds and reservoirs). Each subsection details application, construction approach, and key design considerations.
key_points: Additional seepage barriers include cutoff trenches, foundation grouting, and liners.
Selection depends on whether the application is original construction or remedial, and whether the barrier is in soil or rock.
sections.applicability: Applies when vertical cutoff walls or blankets/berms are not the preferred or feasible solution for seepage control.

sections.title: Cutoff Trench
sections.summary: Describes cutoff trenches as broad, sloped-sidewall excavations backfilled with low-hydraulic-conductivity material, constructed in dam and levee foundations during original construction. Highlights the dual benefit of seepage control and visual inspection of subsurface conditions, and the need for filtered protection on the downstream side to prevent internal erosion.
sections.body: Cutoff trenches are constructed in the foundations of dams and levees as part of the original construction. The cutoffs are generally a broad trench with sloped sidewalls that is backfilled with low hydraulic conductivity material. The trench extends partially or fully through permeable soil and rock layers in the foundation. In addition to the seepage control offered, cutoff trenches provide an opportunity to visually inspect the subsurface conditions beneath the dam or levee. Care should be taken to ensure that the downstream side of the berm is properly filtered (see Section 6-5.3) to prevent internal erosion into permeable foundation soil or rock.
key_points: Cutoff trenches are broad, sloped-wall excavations backfilled with low-k material during original dam/levee construction.
Can partially or fully penetrate permeable foundation layers.
Provide opportunity for visual subsurface inspection during construction.
Downstream side must be properly filtered to prevent internal erosion into the foundation.
sections.applicability: Applies during original dam or levee construction where a broad, excavated cutoff through permeable foundation soils or rock is feasible.

sections.title: Foundation Grouting
sections.summary: Covers cement grouting of bedrock fractures and voids beneath dams to reduce hydraulic conductivity. Describes use of packers to isolate depth intervals, grout curtain configurations with multiple inclined lines to intercept joints, and applicability both as original construction and as a remedial measure.
sections.body: Foundation grouting is performed by pumping stabilized cement grout into boreholes to fill joints and voids in bedrock and reduce the effective hydraulic conductivity of the formation. Foundation grouting can be performed prior to dam construction or after construction as a remedial measure. Grout is pumped into discrete depth intervals of the boring by sealing off an interval using inflatable bladders called packers. Grout lines consisting of evenly spaced boreholes are typically aligned parallel to the axis of the dam although other configurations may be applicable for special circumstances. In many cases, multiple grout lines (grout curtains) are installed along the dam axis with the boreholes inclined in opposite directions to increase the chances of encountering all of the joints and voids in the rock.
key_points: Cement grout is injected into bedrock joints and voids to reduce hydraulic conductivity beneath dams.
Packers isolate discrete depth intervals for controlled grouting.
Grout lines are typically parallel to the dam axis; multiple inclined lines (grout curtains) improve coverage of joints.
Applicable both during original construction and as a post-construction remedial measure.
sections.applicability: Applies when fractured or voided bedrock beneath a dam requires hydraulic conductivity reduction, either as original construction or remedial treatment.

sections.title: Liners
sections.summary: Describes liners for ponds and reservoirs to reduce leakage, including compacted clay, synthetic geomembranes, and native soils amended with bentonite. Notes that uniform foundation conditions are essential to prevent differential settlement from tearing or cracking the liner, analogous to upstream blankets.
sections.body: Leakage from ponds and reservoirs can be reduced by installing a liner in the base of the pond or reservoir. Such liners can consist of compacted clay, synthetic geomembrane liners, or native soils supplemented with bentonite or other materials to reduce hydraulic conductivity. Similar to upstream blankets, the foundation for the liner must be sufficiently uniform to prevent differential settlements under the reservoir loading, which could tear or crack the liner.
key_points: Liner types: compacted clay, synthetic geomembrane, or native soil amended with bentonite.
Uniform foundation is critical — differential settlement under reservoir loading can tear or crack the liner.
Analogous design concern to upstream seepage blankets.
sections.applicability: Applies to ponds and reservoirs where leakage must be minimized by installing a low-permeability base liner.

sections.title: Filters and Drains
sections.summary: Container section covering the design of filters and drainage systems for dams, levees, excavations, and other geotechnical structures. Establishes that drainage elements must provide adequate flow capacity to relieve target pressures and must be filter-compatible with surrounding soils to prevent internal erosion. Subsections cover mineral filters, geotextile filters, surface/subsurface drainage, retaining wall drainage, embankment drains, and foundation drainage.
sections.body:
Drainage systems provide relief of hydraulic pressures in foundations, intercept paths of concentrated seepage, and control the release of the drained water to prevent internal erosion. Properly designed drainage elements will have adequate flow capacity to reduce the pressures for which they are designed while being filter compatible with the surrounding soils to prevent internal erosion through the drainage elements.
Filters and drains are essential components for the drainage systems of a dam, levee, excavation or other geotechnical construction. A filter prevents the migration of the base soil into another soil layer or zone, into a drain, or out of the system through surface flow. The base soil is the material from which the seepage flow is exiting. A drain removes collected water from the collection point to a suitable discharge location. Drains can consist solely of coarse-grained soil that allows rapid seepage through its interstitial voids or can include drainage pipes that collect water from the surrounding coarse-grained drain material.
key_points: Drainage systems must provide adequate flow capacity AND be filter-compatible with adjacent soils.
A filter prevents migration of base soil particles; a drain conveys collected water to a discharge point.
Drains can be coarse-grained soil alone or include slotted/perforated collection pipes.
sections.applicability: Applies to all geotechnical structures requiring seepage pressure relief and/or control of internal erosion through drainage and filtration.

sections.title: Mineral Filter Criteria
sections.summary: Presents a 10-step design procedure (based on FEMA 2011) for graded sand and gravel mineral filters. Covers base soil categorization, retention criteria (maximum D15F based on D85B), flow/permeability criteria (minimum D15F based on D15B), uniformity coefficient requirements, limits on oversized material and fines, segregation criteria, and design for drainpipe perforations. Applicable to critical dam and levee drainage elements.
sections.body:
In order to satisfy its purpose, the filter must (1) have a gradation fine enough to prevent the migration of the base soil into the filter, (2) have high enough hydraulic conductivity to not restrict flow from the base soil, and (3) have the ability to collapse so that cracks in the base soil are not propagated through the filter. Mineral filters consist of sand and gravel that are specifically graded to meet these criteria. Design procedures for mineral filters have been developed by most U.S. agencies involved in dam design. These criteria have been summarized by FEMA (2011). A brief summary of the design procedure is provided in this section.
In the design procedure, the soil being filtered is the base soil and characteristics of the base soil gradation will be followed by a B (e.g. the grain size of which 85 percent of the base soil is passing will be denoted: D85B). Similarly, the filter gradation will be followed by an F (e.g. D15F). Examples of the grain sizes associated with filter design are provided in Figure 6-15.
Based on FEMA (2011), filter design is completed using the following steps:
Step 1. Plot the grain-size distributions for the base soil and assess whether the base soils contain dispersive soils (e.g., soils that disaggregate when in contact with water). ASTM D6572 and D4647 can be used to identify dispersive soils.
Step 2. Assess if the base soil has particles larger than the No. 4 sieve or is gap graded. Gap graded soil may be susceptible to internal instability. Special consideration should be given to a gap graded soil to insure the fine portion of the base soil is protected from erosion.
Step 3. If the base soil contains particles larger than the No. 4 sieve, regrade the grain-size distribution to include only the portion of the distribution finer than the No. 4 sieve. FEMA (2011) provides details on the regrading procedure.
Step 4. Determine the base soil category using Table 6-11.
Step 5. Determine the filter criteria for base soil retention by calculating the maximum D15F based on the criteria in Table 6-12. The retention criteria are based on the principle that the larger particles in the base soil (represented by D85B) must be retained by the voids in the filter (controlled by D15F). By providing a maximum D15F, the criteria ensure that the filter voids are sufficiently small. If the base soil has a range of grain-size distributions, the smallest value of D85B should be used for the retention criteria.
Step 6. Determine the flow criteria for the filter by calculating the minimum D15F based on the criteria in Table 6-13. The permeability criteria are based on the principle that the filter's hydraulic conductivity is strongly related to D15F. By providing a minimum D15F, the filter will have sufficient flow capacity in comparison to the base soil. If the base soil has a range of grain-size distributions, the largest value of D15B should be used for the permeability criteria. Plot the minimum and maximum D15F on a gradation plot and adjust the minimum D15F to ensure that the ratio between the minimum and maximum D15F is not greater than 5 (i.e., Min D15F / Max D15F).
Step 7. Filters should also have a coefficient of uniformity (Cu = D60F / D10F) between 2 and 6.
Step 8. Limit the amount of oversized material and fines in the filter. Most agencies require that the maximum particle size of the filter (D100F) be less than 2 inches (51 mm) although the USACE allows particles up to 3 inches (76 mm). The minimum particle size associated with 5% passing for the filter (D5F) is the No. 200 sieve or 0.075 mm. Any fines present in the filter soil should be non-plastic (i.e., PI = 0).
Step 9. Limit segregation potential of the filter by determining the maximum D90F from Table 6-14. Segregation occurs more easily if a wide range of particle sizes is present.
Step 10. Plot the criteria for minimum D5F, minimum and maximum D15F, maximum D90F, and maximum D100F on a gradation plot to create an acceptable gradation band for the filter. Compare candidate filters with the criteria and gradation band.
Design for Drainpipe Perforations. If the filter is to contain a drainage pipe, the filter soil around the pipe is referred to as the envelope material. The smallest value of D50E (E stands for envelope) allowed by the gradation should be larger than the size of the maximum pipe perforation.
key_points: Mineral filters must satisfy three criteria: particle retention, adequate hydraulic conductivity, and ability to self-heal cracks in the base soil.
Four base soil categories (Table 6-11) based on percent finer than No. 200 sieve; gap-graded soils need special attention.
Retention criterion: maximum D15F controlled by D85B (Table 6-12); dispersive soils use tighter criteria.
Permeability criterion: minimum D15F ≥ (3–5)×D15B depending on agency (Table 6-13); minimum absolute value 0.1 mm.
Filter Cu should be 2–6; D100F < 2 in (51 mm); fines must be non-plastic (PI = 0).
Segregation limits set maximum D90F based on minimum D10F (Table 6-14).
Envelope material D50E must exceed maximum pipe perforation size when a drainpipe is included.
sections.applicability: Applies to design of sand and gravel mineral filters for dams, levees, excavations, and other structures requiring reliable, long-term filtration of base soils.

sections.title: Geotextile Filter Criteria
sections.summary: Covers the design of geotextile filters as alternatives to mineral filters, including retention criteria based on opening size O95, permeability requirements expressed through permittivity (Eq. 6-16), and clogging considerations. Notes that major U.S. dam agencies prohibit geotextile use in critical dam zones due to clogging risk and construction damage potential.
sections.body:
In some cases, geotextiles can be used for soil filtration and drainage in lieu of mineral filters and gravel drains. In general, the FEMA (2011) guidelines do not recommend the use of geotextiles in critical areas of dams. The term geotextiles refers to a wide variety of synthetic, fabric-like products that vary depending on the types of fibers used in the manufacturing and how these fibers are interconnected. The most common forms include woven, nonwoven, and knitted fabrics. Woven geotextiles are manufactured by weaving two perpendicular sets of synthetic fibers to form a fabric. Nonwoven geotextiles have a random orientation often resembling a felt fabric and are manufactured by either needle punching, spun bonding, or resin bonding. Knitted geotextiles consist of interlocking series of loops of fiber yarns that form a fabric.
A common drainage and filtration application for geotextile filter fabrics is a subsurface drain such as presented in Figure 6-17. In this application the drainage is provided by the poorly-graded gravel drainage rock and the slotted outlet pipe. The role of the geotextile is to prevent migration of the surrounding soils into the drainage rock and pipe. In this way, the geotextile prevents erosion of the surrounding soil and/or clogging of the drain. Other applications include drains within retaining wall backfill and drainage blankets below embankments.
For the geotextile fabric in Figure 6-17 or other applications to perform adequately, the geotextile should be designed to have the ability to: (1) retain particles of the base soil to prevent migration through the fabric, (2) allow the passage of water without significant buildup of water pressure, and (3) resist clogging due to accumulation of fine soil particles, chemical precipitates, and biological precipitates.
Criteria for retention of soil particles was proposed by Giroud (2010) based on D20B and the soil's linear coefficient of uniformity (C'u). As shown in Figure 6-18, a log-linear approximation is used to represent the base soil's gradation curve. The linear particle size (D'x) is obtained from the log-linear approximation. The values of D'100 and D'0 are defined by the ends of a straight line drawn through the middle part of the gradation plot (i.e., through D10 and D60).
Geotextiles are designed for retention based on the geotextile opening size (O95), which indicates the size at which 95 percent of openings are smaller. According to Luettich (1992), geotextile retention criteria for soils with less than 10% fines can be selected using the base soil gradation and Table 6-15.
For soils with more than 10% fines and PI greater than 5, the geotextile should have O95 less than 0.21 mm, provided the soil is non-dispersive. For dispersive soils with more than 20% clay sized particles, a filter of 75 to 100 mm of sand should be placed between the base soil and the geotextile, and the geotextile should be designed to retain the filter sand. Retention of non-plastic soils with more than 10% fines can be designed using Table 6-15.
Geotextile filters also must have a much higher hydraulic conductivity than the base soil. A filter cake of trapped particles often forms on the face of a geotextile. These particles must not reduce the hydraulic conductivity of the geotextile to the point that it restricts seepage flow out of the base soil. However, clogging is difficult to quantify. Some clogging will occur when the geotextile is put into service. The geotextile must remain sufficiently open so that accumulation of particles and chemical and biological precipitates will not reduce the hydraulic conductivity to the point where the filter cake/geotextile system becomes less permeable than the base soil. The USBR (2014) recommends the following considerations be taken to assess clogging potential:
• Use the largest opening size that satisfies the retention criterion.
• Do not use geotextile filters in environments where precipitates are likely to form. Avoid high alkalinity groundwater, which can form calcium, sodium, or magnesium precipitates. Also avoid acidic seepage, which can form iron and aluminum hydroxide precipitates.
• Avoid use of geotextiles with internally unstable (Cu > 20) or dispersive soils.
• Avoid organic-rich environments such as agricultural runoff, landfill leachates, and sites known to form iron bacteria.
• Make sure that the geotextile filter makes intimate contact with the soil.
• Do not place geotextile filters against cohesive soils containing voids.
Giroud (2010) suggests that an FSg of 10 to 20 is appropriate to maintain adequate filter permeability. Others (e.g., Loudiere et al. 1983, Christopher and Fischer 1991) recommend that the FSg value be between 10 and 100.
Over the past several decades geotextile filter fabrics have been developed to provide filtration between base soil and coarse-grained drain materials. While these fabrics are inexpensive compared to mineral filters, they are considered by many to be far less reliable than mineral filters due to their propensity to clog and the potential to be damaged during construction. For this reason, all major dam owning and regulating agencies in the U.S. (U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, U.S. Bureau of Reclamation, FEMA, and FERC) do not allow the use of filter fabrics within critical areas of dam embankments or in high-hazard structures.
key_points: Geotextile types: woven, nonwoven (needle-punched, spun-bonded, resin-bonded), and knitted; each has different pore structure and performance.
Retention criterion uses O95 (opening size at which 95% of openings are smaller); Table 6-15 provides criteria for soils with <10% fines.
For soils with >10% fines and PI > 5, O95 < 0.21 mm required (non-dispersive); dispersive soils need an intermediate sand filter layer.
Permeability requirement: kg/ks ≥ FSg, where FSg = 10–100 (Eq. 6-16); permittivity ψg from ASTM D4491.
Clogging is difficult to quantify; avoid alkaline/acidic environments, dispersive soils, and organic-rich settings.
All major U.S. dam agencies prohibit geotextile filters in critical dam embankment zones or high-hazard structures.

equations.description: Geotextile permeability requirement: kg/ks = ψg·tg / ks ≥ FSg, relating geotextile hydraulic conductivity kg, permittivity ψg, thickness tg, base soil hydraulic conductivity ks, and factor of safety FSg.

sections.applicability: Applies when geotextile fabrics are being considered as filter elements in subsurface drains, retaining wall backfill, or drainage blankets (excluding critical dam embankment zones).

sections.title: Surface and Subsurface Drainage
sections.summary: Container section covering drainage solutions for near-surface and surface water management, including intercepting drains for hillside seepage, surface blanket drains for pavement subgrades, drainage of ponded areas using vertical trenches, and retaining wall drainage alternatives. Provides design tools including Figure 6-21 for aggregate base drainage and Figure 6-23 for trench drainage of ponded areas.
sections.body: Pavements and other surface treatments can be destabilized by water ponded at the ground surface or shallow phreatic surfaces. Near-surface groundwater may be collected by intercepting drains prior or collected in the pavement base material as it exits the subgrade. Accumulation of surface water in wide flat areas, due to rainfall or other surface sources, can be mitigated using trench drains connected to deeper drainage systems.
key_points: Near-surface groundwater and surface ponding can destabilize pavements and surface structures.
Intercepting drains, blanket drains, and vertical trench drains address different surface/subsurface drainage scenarios.
Figure 6-21 used to size aggregate base course thickness and drain spacing for pavement drainage.
Figure 6-23 provides trench spacing design for draining ponded areas based on Kirkham (1950, 1960).
sections.applicability: Applies to roadway, pavement, and surface structure drainage design where near-surface groundwater or ponding threatens stability or performance.

sections.title: Intercepting Drains
sections.summary: Describes intercepting (stability) drains — shallow trenches with collector pipes and drainage material — used to intercept horizontal seepage in upper pervious strata on hillsides or near roadways. Covers trench backfill options (mineral filter or geotextile-wrapped aggregate), notes that criticality governs backfill choice, and recommends flow net or FE analysis for drain design.
sections.body: Intercepting drains (a.k.a., stability trenches or stability drains) can be used in locations where water seeping from a hillside has a detrimental effect on slope stability or the performance of roadways. These drains consist of shallow trenches with collector pipes surrounded by drainage material, placed to intercept seepage moving horizontally in an upper pervious stratum as illustrated in Figure 6-19. The trench backfill can consist of a filter material compatible with the surrounding soil as shown in Figure 6-20 or a drainage aggregate wrapped in filter fabric (Figure 6-17). The type of trench backfill and filtering mechanism used will depend on the criticality of the drain. Drain designs should aim to be as simple and constructible as possible while still providing suitable filtering. The effect of intercepting drains on seepage patterns can be evaluated using flow nets or modeled by finite element analyses. Such analyses should also assess the volumetric flow rate into the drains so that the drain pipes and outlets can be properly designed.
key_points: Intercepting drains (stability trenches) intercept horizontal seepage in upper pervious strata to improve slope stability or roadway performance.
Backfill options: mineral filter compatible with surrounding soil or geotextile-wrapped drainage aggregate.
Backfill choice depends on drain criticality; simpler designs preferred where suitable.
Flow nets or FE analyses should be used to evaluate seepage patterns and calculate flow rates for pipe/outlet sizing.
sections.applicability: Applies to hillside or roadway drainage where horizontal seepage in an upper pervious stratum adversely affects slope stability or pavement performance.

sections.title: Surface Blanket Drains
sections.summary: Covers blanket drains used beneath pavements and structures to intercept groundwater and prevent subgrade destabilization or uplift pressure buildup. Design involves calculating flow rate into the blanket to determine outlet spacing and evaluating tolerable uplift pressure. Figure 6-21 provides drainage performance charts for aggregate base course design. Defines effective porosity and its typical range.
sections.body:
Surface blanket drains are used to intercept ground water beneath pavements and structures to mitigate the buildup of water pressure or destabilization of subgrades. In many cases, the aggregate base layer of pavements may be assessed for its effectiveness as a blanket drain. Design of surface blanket drains should consist of: (1) assessment of the flow rate of drainage into the blanket to calculate the needed spacing for outlets and (2) assessment of the tolerable uplift pressure in the blanket to prevent damage to the overlying pavement, embankment, or structure.
The thickness of aggregate base course needed to provide effective drainage can be calculated using Figure 6-21. For a range of slopes, the degree of drainage is related to the porosity and hydraulic conductivity of the aggregate base, the thickness of the base layer, the subgrade slope, the drain spacing, and the time allowed for drainage. Figure 6-21 can be used to select drain spacing or evaluate suitability of base material.
Effective porosity (also called specific yield) is the quantity of water per unit volume that is not retained in the soil by capillarity during discharge (Barber 1959). It ranges from 25 percent for a uniform material, such as medium to coarse sand, to 15 percent for a well-graded sand-gravel mixture.
key_points: Blanket drains beneath pavements require two design checks: flow rate for outlet spacing and tolerable uplift pressure.
Figure 6-21 relates drainage degree to aggregate base porosity, hydraulic conductivity, thickness, slope, drain spacing, and drainage time.
Effective porosity (specific yield) ranges from ~15% (well-graded sand-gravel) to ~25% (uniform medium-coarse sand).
Existing aggregate base layers may be evaluated for adequacy as blanket drains.
sections.applicability: Applies to design of aggregate base drainage layers beneath pavements and structures where subgrade groundwater buildup or uplift pressure is a concern.

sections.title: Drainage of Ponded Areas
sections.summary: Describes use of vertical drainage trenches to mitigate ponding in flat or enclosed basins. Figure 6-23 (after Kirkham 1950, 1960) provides flow rate estimates into parallel trenches for cases with fully pervious or impervious underlying zones, enabling design of trench spacing (2×S) to meet required surface infiltration. Notes that insufficient trench capacity requires surface drainage facilities.
sections.body: During times of heavy rainfall or runoff from adjacent areas, vertical drainage trenches can be used to mitigate ponding water in level areas or enclosed basins. The flow rate of seepage into parallel trenches can be estimated using Figure 6-23 for an underlying zone that is either completely pervious or completely impervious in comparison to the surface layer. The trench spacing (2×S) can be designed such that the calculated flow rate into the trenches meets or exceeds the required surface infiltration for an area of 1×2×S. The trench must also be designed to sustain the required flow rate and may include collector pipes. If sufficient drainage capacity cannot be provided using trenches, surface drainage facilities are required to prevent ponding.
key_points: Vertical drainage trenches drain ponded water in flat or enclosed areas.
Figure 6-23 (Kirkham 1950, 1960) estimates seepage flow rate into parallel trenches for pervious or impervious underlying conditions.
Trench spacing (2×S) selected so calculated inflow meets required surface infiltration for each drainage area (1×2×S).
If trench capacity is insufficient, surface drainage facilities are required.
sections.applicability: Applies to design of vertical trench drainage systems for mitigating ponding in flat or low-lying areas during heavy rainfall or runoff events.

sections.title: DEWATERING
sections.summary: Introduces dewatering as the practice of lowering groundwater to enable subsurface construction or protect existing facilities. Covers the three primary dewatering options—sump collection, wellpoint systems, and deep extraction wells—and notes that system selection depends on expected inflows, heave potential, and required depth of drawdown. Specialized engineering firms are available for dewatering design.
sections.body: Sometimes it is necessary to lower the groundwater level to allow for subsurface construction or to prevent flooding of existing facilities. Dewatering options include: (1) a collection system at the base of the excavation leading to a sump, (2) a well point system, and (3) deep extraction wells. The selection of a dewatering system depends on the expected inflows into the excavation, the potential for heave (see Section 6-4.1), and the required depth of groundwater lowering. There are engineering firms and consultants that specialize in dewatering.
key_points: Dewatering is used to lower groundwater for subsurface construction or to protect existing facilities.
Three main dewatering options: sump collection, wellpoint systems, and deep extraction wells.
System selection is governed by expected inflow volume, heave potential, and required drawdown depth.
Specialized dewatering engineering firms and consultants are available.
sections.applicability: Applies whenever groundwater must be lowered to facilitate subsurface construction or protect facilities from flooding.

sections.title: Collection and Sump
sections.summary: Describes the collection-and-sump dewatering method, appropriate for excavations in low-hydraulic-conductivity soils where inflow is small and heave is not a concern. Collection trenches or relief trenches channel water to a sump equipped with an electric or gasoline-powered pump. A poorly-graded gravel layer may also be placed over the excavation bottom as a temporary measure.
sections.body: When the volume of inflow into an excavation is low (i.e., excavation into low hydraulic conductivity soils) and the potential for heave is not a concern, a collection and sump system may be sufficient. The collection system may consist of a series of trenches on the bottom of the excavation or a system of relief trenches (see Section 6-5.3.3.1) at the base of the excavation. In some temporary cases, a layer of poorly-graded gravel can be placed over the bottom of the excavation that allows water to flow toward the sump. The collection system leads to a sump with a pump to remove the inflow. Sump pumps can be either electric or gasoline-powered (i.e., "trash" pumps).
key_points: Collection-and-sump is suitable for low-inflow excavations in low-hydraulic-conductivity soils where heave is not a concern.
Collection trenches or relief trenches at the excavation base channel water to the sump.
A temporary poorly-graded gravel layer can be placed over the excavation bottom to direct flow toward the sump.
Sump pumps may be electric or gasoline-powered ('trash' pumps).
sections.applicability: Applies to excavations in low-hydraulic-conductivity soils with low inflow volumes and no significant heave risk.

sections.title: Wellpoint Systems
sections.summary: Covers wellpoint dewatering systems, which use 1-1/2- or 2-inch slotted/screened pipes connected to suction headers. Effective for soils with D10 > 0.05 mm or soils with laminated structure. Maximum drawdown is limited to 15–18 ft below the suction header due to atmospheric pressure constraints; staged installations can achieve greater depths. Spacing, discharge, and analysis methods are discussed.
sections.body:
Wellpoints are 1-1/2- or 2-inch diameter pipes that are connected to a suction system to remove the groundwater. The lower section of each wellpoint is slotted or perforated and screened to prevent removal of the surrounding soil into the pipe. The pipes are pushed or jetted in place, or installed in predrilled holes. The wellpoints are each connected to a header leading to suction pumps.

Wellpoints are generally effective when the soil has D10 greater than 0.05 mm or if the soil has a structure, such as varves or laminations, for conducting groundwater horizontally. The maximum differential pressure that can be developed in wellpoints is limited by atmospheric pressure. Thus, the drawdown of the groundwater level using wellpoints is ordinarily limited to 15 to 18 feet below the center of the suction header. If a greater amount of drawdown is required, wellpoints can be installed in successive tiers or stages as excavation proceeds as illustrated in Figure 6-31.

The discharge capacity for each wellpoint is generally 15 to 30 gpm (3 to 6 m3/hour). Wellpoint spacing is typically between 3 and 10 feet (1 and 3 m). Closer spacing should be used for soils with lower hydraulic conductivity. In such soils, the effectiveness of wellpoints can be increased by predrilling the locations and backfilling with sand around the wellpoint.

Due to the close spacing of wellpoints, a two-dimensional analysis is generally sufficient. The drawdown and flow into the line of wellpoints can be analyzed either with a flow net or two-dimensional finite element analysis. For soil with high k (clean fine sand or coarser), the quantity of water to be removed controls wellpoint layout. For silty soils, the flow rate is relatively small, and the number and spacing of wellpoints will be influenced by the time available to accomplish dewatering.
key_points: Wellpoints are 1-1/2- or 2-inch slotted/screened pipes connected to suction headers; installed by pushing, jetting, or predrilling.
Effective for soils with D10 > 0.05 mm or those with laminated/varved structure allowing horizontal groundwater flow.
Atmospheric pressure limits drawdown to 15–18 ft below the suction header; staged/tiered installation required for deeper drawdown.
Discharge capacity per wellpoint: 15–30 gpm (3–6 m³/hr); typical spacing 3–10 ft (1–3 m).
Closer spacing and sand backfill around predrilled holes improves effectiveness in low-k silty soils.
Two-dimensional analysis (flow net or FEM) is generally sufficient due to close wellpoint spacing.
High-k soils: pumping quantity controls layout. Silty soils: time for dewatering controls number and spacing.
sections.applicability: Applies to excavation dewatering projects where soils have D10 > 0.05 mm or laminated structure, and required drawdown is within suction limits or staged installation is feasible.

sections.title: Extraction Wells
sections.summary: Describes deep extraction wells for dewatering, covering their construction (bored hole, casing, screen, filter pack, turbine or submersible pump) and four key use cases: external system placement, large long-term pumping, pre-excavation drawdown, and pressure relief in confined aquifers. Also addresses ejector/eductor pumps as an alternative for lifts up to 60 ft, and references Figure 6-32 for drawdown and pumping quantity calculations.
sections.body:
Extraction wells consist of a bored hole containing a well casing with a screened section in the aquifer, a filter pack, and a pipe column. A turbine-type pump with a motor at the surface can be used, or a submersible pump may be placed within the well casing. Extraction wells are used if (a) the dewatering system must be kept outside the excavation area, (b) large quantities of water must be pumped for a long period of time, (c) pumping must commence before excavation to obtain the necessary time for drawdown, or (d) pressures must be lowered in a confined aquifer that is below a low-permeability layer underlying an excavation. Extraction wells may be used for soils with classifications ranging from gravel to silty fine sand, and for water bearing rocks. Bored shallow wells with suction pumps can be used to replace wellpoints where pumping is required for several months or in silty soils where correct filtering is critical.

Ejector or eductor pumps may be utilized within wellpoints for lifts up to about 60 feet. The ejector pump has a nozzle arrangement at the bottom of two small diameter riser pipes which remove water by the Venturi principle. They are used in lieu of a multistage wellpoint system and if the large pumping capacity provided by extraction wells is not required. Their primary application is for sands, but with proper control they can also be used in silty sands and sandy silts.

Figure 6-32 presents equations for analysis of drawdown and pumping quantities for single wells or a group of wells in a circular pattern. The radius of influence (R) is often defined as the radius beyond which the well has no influence. R is a function of the discharge (q) and thus changes depending on the rate of pumping. The equations presented allow the calculation of R from data in a single observation well. Once R is known, drawdown at other locations can be calculated.
key_points: Extraction wells use a bored casing with screen, filter pack, and either a surface turbine pump or submersible pump.
Used when: system must be outside excavation, large long-term pumping needed, pre-excavation drawdown required, or confined aquifer pressure must be relieved.
Applicable for soils from gravel to silty fine sand and water-bearing rocks.
Ejector/eductor pumps (Venturi principle) provide lifts up to ~60 ft and serve as alternative to multistage wellpoints for sands, silty sands, and sandy silts.
Figure 6-32 provides equations for drawdown and pumping quantities for single wells and circular well groups.
Radius of influence (R) depends on discharge rate (q) and can be calculated from a single observation well; once known, drawdown anywhere can be determined.
sections.applicability: Applies when large-scale or long-duration dewatering is needed, when the system must remain outside the excavation, or when confined aquifer pressure relief is required.

sections.title: Suggested Reading
sections.summary: Provides a curated list of reference texts for Chapter 6 topics including groundwater flow, filter design, and numerical seepage analysis. References span foundational textbooks (Cedergren 1977, Freeze & Cherry 1979), FEMA guidance on embankment dam filters (2011), and finite element analysis resources for geotechnical practice (Bradley & VandenBerge 2015; Potts & Zdravkovic 2001).
sections.body:
Topic | Reference
Groundwater Flow | Cedergren, H. R. 1977. Seepage, Drainage, and Flow Nets, John Wiley and Sons, Inc., New York.
Groundwater Flow | Freeze, R. A. and Cherry, J.A. 1979. Groundwater Prentice-Hall, Englewood Cliffs, NJ.
Filter Design | Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), 2011. Filters for Embankment Dams, Best Practices for Design and Construction.
Numerical Seepage Analysis | Bradley, N. and VandenBerge, D. R. 2015. Beginner's Guide for Geotechnical Finite Element Analyses, Center for Geotechnical Practice and Research, Virginia Tech.
Numerical Seepage Analysis | Potts, D. M. and Zdravkovic, L. 2001. Finite Element Analysis in Geotechnical Engineering: Theory and Application ICE Publishing.
key_points: Cedergren (1977) is the foundational reference for seepage, drainage, and flow net construction.
Freeze & Cherry (1979) is the standard reference for groundwater flow theory.
FEMA (2011) provides best practices for filter design in embankment dams.
Bradley & VandenBerge (2015) and Potts & Zdravkovic (2001) cover numerical (finite element) seepage analysis methods.
sections.applicability: Applies when an engineer needs authoritative references for groundwater flow theory, filter design, or numerical seepage analysis covered in Chapter 6.

sections.title: Notation
sections.summary: Defines all symbols and abbreviations used throughout Chapter 6 on seepage and groundwater flow. Covers hydraulic parameters (head, gradient, conductivity, flow rate), soil particle size descriptors used in filter and Kozeny-Carman equations, geotextile design parameters (permittivity, apparent opening size, hydraulic conductivity), and flow net quantities (Nd, Nf, equipotential drops).
sections.body:
Symbol | Description
a | Isotropic transformation factor for flow nets
A | Cross sectional area of the flow region perpendicular to the flow direction
Cʹu | Linear coefficient of uniformity (geotextile design)
Dli | Particle size of the coarser sieve (Kozeny-Carman equation)
Dsi | Particle size of the finer sieve (cm)
Dα | Effective grain size - α is the percent of soil particles smaller than the stated size, values of 5, 10, 15, and 20 are commonly used for α
Dx | Particle size for which X% of the soil is finer
Dʹx | Particle size for which X% of the soil is finer for linearized particle distribution (geotextile design)
DxB | Particle size for which X% of the soil is finer for a base soil
DxF | Particle size for which X% of the soil is finer for a filter material
e | Void ratio of the soil
fi | Fraction of particles between two adjacent sieve sizes (Kozeny-Carman equation)
FSg | Factor of safety for geotextile permeability
hL | Head loss across flow region
hp | Pressure head
ht | Total hydraulic head
hv | Velocity head
hz | Elevation head
i | Hydraulic gradient
k | Hydraulic conductivity of soil (various subscripts)
kg | Hydraulic conductivity of geotextile across plane of fabric
L | Length of flow path
n | Porosity of the soil
Nd | Number of equipotential (head) drops in the flow net
Nf | Number of flow channels in the flow net
O95 | Geotextile apparent opening size
q | Volumetric flow rate
R | Radius of influence in well design
S | Surface area factor for grain shape (Kozeny-Carman equation)
tg | Geotextile thickness
u | Water pressure at the point of interest
vd | Discharge velocity
vs | Seepage velocity
x | Exponent on effective grain size for hydraulic conductivity correlations
Y | Height of the flow region
Z | Elevation of a point of interest above the elevation datum
βα | Empirical or semi-empirical coefficient relating k to Dα
γw | Unit weight of water
∆hl | Total head loss for one equipotential drop on a flow net
ψg | Geotextile permittivity, provided by manufacturers or from testing (ASTM D4491)
key_points: Hydraulic head components are defined: total head (ht), pressure head (hp), elevation head (hz), and velocity head (hv).
Particle size notation distinguishes base soil (DxB), filter material (DxF), effective grain size (Dα), and linearized distribution (Dʹx) for geotextile design.
Flow net quantities Nd (number of equipotential drops) and Nf (number of flow channels) are key inputs for seepage flow rate calculations.
Geotextile-specific symbols include permittivity (ψg), apparent opening size (O95), hydraulic conductivity (kg), thickness (tg), and factor of safety (FSg).
Kozeny-Carman equation variables include Dli (coarser sieve size), Dsi (finer sieve size), fi (fraction between sieves), and S (surface area factor for grain shape).
βα is an empirical/semi-empirical coefficient used to relate hydraulic conductivity k to effective grain size Dα.
sections.applicability: Applies whenever interpreting equations, figures, or tables in Chapter 6 that use symbolic notation for seepage, filter design, or geotextile analyses.
